11123-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Kuno Francke edited this first volume of The German Classics of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries, published at Albany in 1913, in twenty illustrated volumes. The volume opens with a general introduction by Richard M. Meyer and a life of Goethe by Calvin Thomas, followed by Goethe's poems in English translation: Greeting and Departure, The Heathrose, Prometheus, The Erl-King, Mignon, and many more.

Longer works follow: Hermann and Dorothea, translated by Ellen Frothingham, and Iphigenia in Tauris, translated by Anna Swanwick, with the Faust legend traced from Marlowe to Goethe. In Iphigenia, Arkas urges the heroine not to shake a spirit he cannot bend, and she answers that his labour only occasions pain. The volume gives English readers the masterpieces of German literature in scholarly, readable translations.
11143-mary-marie:
Eleanor H. Porter published this 1920 novel, Mary Marie, illustrated by Helen Mason Grose. The narrator explains her name at once: father calls me Mary, mother calls me Marie, everybody else calls me Mary Marie, and the rest of her name is Anderson. She is thirteen, and, as nurse Sarah says, a cross-current and a contradiction, since her father and mother are unlikes.

Now she will live half the time with mother in Boston and half with father at home, a divorce, you know, which excites her. Chapters follow her birth, Nurse Sarah's story, the break, when I am Marie, when I am Mary, when I am both together, and which is the real love story. Porter tells a divorce story through a girl's cheerful, observant voice.
11366-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume two of the German Classics, Masterpieces of German Literature in twenty volumes, is devoted to Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, published in 1914. Contents center on Elective Affinities, translated by Froude and Boylan, with essays on Shakespeare, an oration on Wieland. the Pedagogic Province from Wilhelm Meister's Travels, Winckelmann and His Age, maxims and reflections, Eckermann's conversations, and correspondence with Humboldt and Zelter.

Calvin Thomas introduces Elective Affinities, and illustrations show Edward reading to Charlotte, Ottilie examining presents, Goethe's study, and Weimar scenes. The volume presents Goethe as novelist, critic, and correspondent together. For English readers, it was a standard gateway to Goethe before modern translations replaced it.
11503-keeping-up-with-lizzie:
Irving Bacheller's 1911 comic novel follows Lizzie, a young woman from Pointview who returns home having met a queen, picked up an accent, and gained a fiancé. The leading tradesmen of the town, turned into a board of assessors, open the fun.

Later chapters bring a ham war, Lizzie's sway over the rich and great, a duel with automobiles, and the Honourable Socrates Potter catching up with her at last. Told in a country voice, the book pokes gentle fun at new money, new manners, and a small town trying to keep pace with one lively girl.
11692-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume three of The German Classics, published in 1914, is devoted to Friedrich von Schiller. Calvin Thomas writes his life at the start. Poems follow, from To the Ideal and The Veiled Image at Saïs to The Glove and The Diver.

The Cranes of Ibycus and The Lay of the Bell appear as well. Dramas include The Death of Wallenstein, translated by Coleridge. History brings the Thirty Years' War and the last campaigns of Gustavus Adolphus. Schiller's letters to Goethe close the literary section. A passage on Swiss men joining hands as one people shows the drama's patriotic fire.
12040-beaumont-and-fletcher-s-works-vol-:
Volume 2 of Beaumont and Fletcher's works presents The Humourous Lieutenant, a tragicomedy, with its persons represented. King Antigonus is an old man with young desires, his son Demetrius is in love with Celia. Seleucus, Lysimachus, and Ptolemy are three kings, equal sharers with Antigonus of what Alexander had, now united against him.

Leontius, a brave old merry soldier and assistant to Demetrius, anchors the play's comic energy, with Timon, Charinthus, and Menippus among the supporting figures. Beaumont and Fletcher's tragicomedy mixes love, war, and humor in the Jacobean manner, where a king's desire and a soldier's jest can turn a political crisis into a play.
12060-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume four of a twenty-volume English set issued in 1914, the volume samples German writing from the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries. Jean Paul, the Schlegel brothers, Novalis, Holderlin, Tieck, and Kleist all appear, most in fresh translations made for the series.

Readers meet Jean Paul comic village tales and Humboldt on Schiller growth as a thinker. Schlegel lectures on drama appear beside Kleist novella Michael Kohlhaas, about a horse dealer whose quest for justice turns violent. Short poems, aphorisms, and fairy tales by Tieck and Novalis fill out the picture. The volume works as a guided tour of German Romantic thought, where feeling, imagination, and moral law pull against each other.
12351-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume seven of The German Classics, patrons edition in twenty volumes, appeared in 1914 from the German Publication Society. The volume gathers Hegel, Bettina von Arnim, Immermann, Gutzkow, Grun, Lenau, Morike, Droste-Hulshoff, Freiligrath, Strachwitz, Geibel, and Herwegh.

Contents mix philosophy, lyric poetry, and fiction, with Hegel thought beside Morike lyrics and Droste-Hulshoff verse. A mid-book passage follows a hunter and Lisbeth at a church door, shy and silent, in a tale of village love. The volume shows German literature between Romanticism and realism, where feeling meets social change. For English readers, it offers a guided sample of writers seldom met outside anthologies.
12473-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume six of The German Classics, a twenty-volume English series issued in 1914, gives Heinrich Heine, Franz Grillparzer and Ludwig van Beethoven. Heine comes first, with a life by William Guild Howard and poems in many translators' hands. Songs, a lyrical intermezzo, sonnets, Poor Peter, The Two Grenadiers and The Pilgrimage to Kevlaar are among them.

Grillparzer and Beethoven follow, joining lyric poetry to drama and to music, so the volume spans three arts in one binding. The many translators, from Sir Theodore Martin to Elizabeth Barrett Browning, show an age keen to bring German writing to English readers. As an anthology it remains a useful door into Heine's wit and feeling, and into his neighbours' work.
12573-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume eight of The German Classics, 1914, edited with an essay by Edwin C. Roedder on the novel of provincial life, gives Auerbach, Gotthelf, Reuter, Stifter and Riehl. Auerbach's Little Barefoot, translated by Dulcken and revised by Thomas, opens the fiction, followed by Gotthelf's Uli, the Farmhand, in translations and synopses by Morgan.

Reuter's Bräsig episodes from Ut mine Stromtid, Stifter's Rock Crystal, and Riehl's Field and Forest, Eye for Natural Scenery and Musical Ear complete the volume. Translators and editors abridge and shape the texts for English readers. The anthology offers a window on German village life, in stories of farms, forests and small towns.
12888-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume five of The German Classics, patrons' edition of 1914, gathers masterpieces of German literature in English translation. Special writers cover the romantic philosophers Fichte, Schelling, and Schleiermacher, plus later German romanticism, while translators render Uhland, Arnim, Brentano, and the Grimms. Poems, tales, and essays share the volume.

A long passage on Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm praises Jacob's grammar and history of language, and Wilhelm's more romantic gift for synthesis under poetic stress. Their folk-tale work, begun under Arnim's influence, anchors the book. The volume offers a rich, old-style gateway to German letters.
12890-elizabethan-demonology-an-essay-in:
Thomas Alfred Spalding's Elizabethan Demonology, published in 1880 and dedicated to Robert Browning, studies belief in devils during the Reformation and after, with special reference to Shakespeare. The essay grew from two papers read before the New Shakspere Society in 1877 and 1878, on the witches in Macbeth and on Shakespeare's demonology. Globe edition references guide the text.

Spalding quotes a devil who turns hound, hog, headless bear, and fire by turns, and notes a 1584 Somerset tale of a devil in the likeness of a headless bear. He warns against dismissing ancestors as fools for their witchcraft creed. The book suits readers of Shakespeare, folklore, and Reformation thought.
13030-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume nine of The German Classics, patrons' edition of 1914, pairs Friedrich Hebbel with Otto Ludwig. Hebbel's Maria Magdalena, Siegfried's Death, Anna, and journal extracts appear, with a life by William Guild Howard. Ludwig's Hereditary Forester and Between Heaven and Earth appear with a life by Alexander Hohlfeld. Translators include Paul Bernard Thomas and Katherine Royce.

A Hebbel passage on poetry warns against penning up free life in tyrannical generalities, lest a stream fit for bathing congeal into a sledge road. The volume gives English readers two major German dramatists. It suits students of nineteenth-century German literature.
13056-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume ten of The German Classics, in the 1914 patrons' edition, gathers Prince Otto von Bismarck, Count Helmuth von Moltke, and Ferdinand Lassalle in English. Bismarck's section leads with Kuno Francke's essay on him as a national type, then love letters, letters with William I, thoughts and recollections, and speeches. Titles include We Shall Never Go to Canossa and Bismarck as the Honest Broker.

Bismarck recalls school at Plamann's, run on Jahn's drill system, and his boyhood view that Brutus and Tell were criminals. A later travel passage tells of a boat sucked toward a Tigris whirlpool, with icy water breaking over the crew. The volume mixes statesmanship, memoir, and travel, and it serves as an English door into German political prose.
13501-lady-connie:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1916 novel Lady Connie follows Constance through three parts, from country houses and tea parties to university discipline and tangled affections. Connie sits in the shadow of a plane tree with Falloden at her feet, listens entranced to Radowitz playing, and sits beside him in silence.

Falloden argues that a man who never went to public school must be disciplined at university, and that Otto Radowitz, as an artist, needs it most, though he never means his impertinences. Winifred recalls Douglas breaking a hunting whip on a labourer's boy, while Marcia calls it high spirits. Ward writes of class, art, and marriage with the moral seriousness of her later novels.
13694-mince-pie:
Christopher Morley gathered these light essays and sketches under the title Mince Pie. Most first appeared in Philadelphia and Boston newspapers and in magazines such as Life and The Smart Set. Morley jokes that the book should be read in bed, and only from a copy the reader has bought. The tone stays playful from the first page.

Subjects range from books and bookshops to city streets, holidays, and odd human habits. Morley praises old volumes, mocks modern fuss, and tells small stories with a smile. A note on a Poe volume bought for a large sum shows his love of literary lore. The pieces are short and easy to dip into. They offer a cheerful view of American letters after the First World War.
13740-mischievous-maid-faynie:
Laura Jean Libbey wrote this 1899 romance around a bold young woman named Faynie. The story opens in a New York blizzard, where two young men brave snow and sleet on Broadway. Faynie soon charms, teases, and unsettles the men around her. Her mischief drives the plot from drawing rooms to grand houses on the hills.

Libbey builds the tale from secrets, rival suitors, and sudden reversals of fortune. Faynie's wit keeps her ahead of gossip and scheming relatives. Lester Armstrong, one of her admirers, watches her with growing devotion. The novel moves fast and leans on strong feeling rather than fine detail. It is a good sample of popular American romance at the end of the 1800s.
13993-dere-mable-love-letters-of-a-rooki:
Edward Streeter wrote Dere Mable, love letters of a rookie, in 1918, with illustrations by G. William Breck. Bill, a private in the 27th New York Division, writes home to Mable in comic misspelling. He dedicates the book to a million Private Bills who learnt to call a coat a blouse. They grumble by custom, stay cheerful by nature, and serve as a matter of course.

Bill does not know his address and asks Mable to write care of the general. He thanks her mother for a red muffler and signs relentlessly yours. Letters joke about army life, food, and homesickness. The book became a wartime hit. It suits readers of First World War humour and American slang.
14018-marie:
Laura E. Richards, author of Captain January, wrote Marie in 1894 as a romance of France and America. Marie, tired after walking nearly all day, watches low sun rays strike farmhouse windows into flame. She thinks the rays like fiddle-bows over tree-tops and slopes. Chapters follow Marie, d'Arthenay, Abby Rock, possession, and courtship.

D'Arthenay, like most of his race in the tale, scorns earthly life and broods on heaven and hell. He leaves castle and lands behind with his wife. Later chapters bring wedlock, looking back, a flower in snow, and vita nuova. Richards writes with gentle sentiment and French colour. The novel suits readers of late Victorian romance.
14470-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Volume twelve of The German Classics, edited by Kuno Francke of Harvard and published in Albany in 1914, pairs Gustav Freytag with Theodor Fontane. The twenty-volume series offered masterpieces of German literature in English translation.

Freytag's life and work open the volume, with essays on Frederick the Great and his age, while Fontane's fiction and criticism follow. Contributors and translators, many of them American professors, supply introductions and notes. The volume gives English readers a scholarly gateway to two major nineteenth-century German writers. Francke's Harvard series aimed at a wide American audience.
14534-christmas-with-grandma-elsie:
Martha Finley's 1888 Christmas book returns to Grandma Elsie Travilla at Ion, where November ice and snow glitter on trees and walks as the family gathers for the holiday. Rosie and Walter open the story with morning greetings.

Skating feats on the ice, old gentlemen recalling their youth, and Christmas preparations fill the chapters, with Grandma Elsie presiding over prayer and affection. Finley's tone is warm and pious, in the Elsie series' familiar manner. Young readers of the series met old friends again at Ion. The book offers a gentle, old-fashioned Christmas, centered on home, faith, and family togetherness.
14617-poems-c-1790-wherein-it-is-attempt:
This 1790 London volume of poems, printed for J. Johnson in St. Paul's Churchyard, attempts to describe views of nature and rustic manners. It also shows how the same circumstances affect different characters. A winter day opens the book.

A cock crows on the roost, and a laborer dreams of next year's crop and wool bargains. A musing youth, deaf to chickens, rooks, and cows, thinks only of Nelly, the blithest village maid. The verse is plain and observant, in the manner of late Georgian descriptive poetry. The collection offers a quiet window on country life before Romanticism.
14763-winston-of-the-prairie:
Harold Bindloss sets this 1907 romance on the Canadian prairie, where rancher Winston works hard ground, hard winters and harder neighbours. Lance Courthorne, Trooper Shannon and Maud Barrington enter his orbit, bringing rivalry, quarrels and a promise that will test him.

At Silverdale, Winston must prove mastery of his land and of himself. Chapters move from ranch labour and the speed of the plough to an armistice, a fair advocate and a sudden crisis that ends facing the flame. Bindloss writes prairie life in plain, muscular prose, and the love story runs through it without softening the work. The result is an adventure of settlement, pride and second chances.
14883-grandmother-elsie:
Martha Finley's Grandmother Elsie, a sequel to Elsie's Widowhood, finds the Ion family home again after a summer on the New Jersey coast. Early October brings dew on green grass, bright waters on a lakelet, a rowboat at a little wharf, gardens gay with flowers and trees in autumn dress.

Elsie, now a grandmother, guides children and grandchildren through joy and sorrow, in the mingled yarn of good and ill that Shakespeare's line promises. The complete authorised edition, published by arrangement with Dodd, Mead, keeps Finley's moral household at its centre. Readers of the series will recognise the faith, family talk and gentle discipline that made Elsie a household name.
15544-love-letters-of-a-rookie-to-julie:
Barney Stone, of Headquarters Company, 119th Field Artillery, American Expeditionary Force, published these love letters in 1919, with pictures by Gordon Ross. They are written in a rookie's broad comic dialect, addressed to Julie back home. The dedication credits R. E. S., whose suggestions made the pages possible and palatable.

The first letter finds Stone in camp, somewhere between the kitchen and the lunch counter, after being rough-housed on the rattlers for a day and two nights. He recalls a fond farewell in Julie's hallway, spoiled by a neighbor on the second floor whose bell she backed into. The letters mix camp humor, homesickness, and sweet talk, in the voice of a doughboy writing home while the war still shapes his days.
16268-the-story-of-jessie:
Mabel Quiller-Couch's Story of Jessie opens at Sunnyside Cottage, where Thomas Dawson tries to make the kettle boil and toast bread in a tidy kitchen. Through the dewy, sunny garden, green filming over brown branches, he spots Daniel Magor the postman at the gate, and a letter for the cottage changes the household's day. Contents follow Jessie arriving, shopping and teaing, a garden Sunday school, and happy days.

Taken by surprise, a journey and arrival, a new home, Miss Patch, Charlie reaching home, too late, and Springbrook again complete the tale. Quiller-Couch writes gentle, domestic fiction for young readers, full of cottages, gardens, and kind neighbors. Children will enjoy Jessie's small adventures and warm homecoming.
1631-a-monk-of-fife-being-the-chronicle-:
Andrew Lang's Monk of Fife, done into English out of the French, presents the chronicle of Norman Leslie of Pitcullo, concerning marvellous deeds in France in 1429 to 1431. A young Scot becomes a monk, flees his order, and finds himself amid the wars of Joan of Arc, with sieges, visions, and chivalry along the way.

The chronicle blends history with romance, and Lang's translation keeps its old-world flavour. Norman's tale moves from Fife to France and back to memory. The book is a charming historical romance, and a tribute to Joan's age told by a Scotsman who claims to have been there.
1641-the-lesser-bourgeoisie:
Balzac's Lesser Bourgeoisie, also called The Middle Classes, follows the lesser bourgeois of Paris through a novel of manners and morals. Clerks, small officials, and their families scheme for places, pensions, and marriages, while departing Paris and returning ambition shape a crowded social comedy.

Dedicated to Constance-Victoire, the book watches middle-class life with Balzac's usual appetite for detail and motive. Its characters are neither grand nor poor, but anxiously in between. The novel is a rich, unfinished-seeming portrait of the class that keeps Paris running and worrying.
16420-the-arte-of-english-poesie:
Printed in London in 1589, this is the first great English handbook of poetry, in three books: of poets and poetry, of proportion, and of ornament. The printer's dedication to Lord Burghley notes the book came to hand without an author's name, though passages show it was meant for Queen Elizabeth's recreation and service.

The text teaches how to shape verse, choose figures, and suit style to subject, with examples from court life. It stands at the start of English criticism, written when poetry was a courtly art. Scholars and poets still turn to it for the earliest rules of English verse in action.
16528-forty-one-years-in-india-from-suba:
This memoir covers forty-one years in India, from subaltern to commander-in-chief, first published in January 1897 in two volumes and reprinted again and again within weeks. Early chapters tell of a voyage to India, life in Calcutta, a destructive cyclone, and homesickness, then Bengal Horse Artillery, Peshawar in 1852, frontier fights, and a trip to Kashmir.

The writer served through the great events of British India, from frontier stations to high command. The memoir is long, detailed, and soldierly, with campaigns and stations in full. Readers of imperial military history will find a first-hand life spanning the Raj's most active decades.
16622-literary-hearthstones-of-dixie:
La Salle Corbell Pickett wrote this 1912 book of southern writers seen at home, issued by Lippincott in Philadelphia and London. With portraits and pictures, it visits hearths where writers of the old South gave friends welcome and talk. Augusta Evans Wilson's Ashland Place leads the set of homes and lives.

Pickett writes with warmth about talk by the fire, where thoughts long shut in found words and went out to the world. The book is part travel, part memoir, part literary life, and it keeps a vanished social world in view. Readers who love southern letters will enjoy its homes, its hosts, and its gentle, backward look.
16969-dick-and-brownie:
Mabel Quiller-Couch's children's tale opens on a hot moor road, where a caravan holds a cruel man and woman, a starved horse, and a dog. Dick and Brownie, the dog at the heart of the book, escape that hard life and find kinder folk, including Miss Rose. Night scares, a shopping trip, a rescue, and a new home follow across twelve chapters.

The story pleads, in plain scenes, for kind care of beasts and for pluck in young readers. Huldah's path from fear to a happy home gives the book its warmth. Written in simple, vivid prose, it remains a gentle animal tale with a firm moral and a happy, earned close.
16993-miss-dexie:
Stanford Eveleth's 1895 romance opens in a New England town during the Civil War, when death lists and street talk of Spotsylvania fill the air. Miss Dexie, the heroine of the provinces, grows through war years, home trials, and love, as kin and neighbors weigh duty, pride, and hope. The Toronto imprint marks it as a Canadian tale of American scenes.

Long and earnest, the novel mixes domestic drama with the national wound of its age. Its chapters move from parting and loss to steadier joys, in the plain style of late-1800s popular fiction. Readers who like period romance with a historic frame will find a full, heartfelt story here.
17439-mother-s-remedies-over-one-thousan:
Dr. T. J. Ritter, formerly connected with the medical faculty of the University of Michigan at Ann Arbor, compiled this home remedy book, published in Detroit in 1921 with revisions by Dr. W. E. Ziegenfuss. Its title promises over one thousand tried and tested remedies from mothers of the United States and Canada. It also covers symptoms, causes, prevention, diet, nursing, and treatments for every known disease, with sections on poisons, accidents, herbs, women, children, and infants.

Modern readers should treat the book as history, not advice. Its transcriber warns that many recipes include kerosene, turpentine, lead, lye, strychnine, arsenic, mercury, opium, and cocaine, and that some do not say whether they are for skin or for swallowing. The volume remains valuable as a record of household medicine before modern drugs.
17735-eyes-of-youth-a-book-of-verse-by-p:
Young poets gather in this book of verse, Eyes of Youth, with a foreword by G. K. Chesterton. Contributors include Padraic Colum, Shane Leslie, Viola Meynell, Ruth Lindsay, Hugh Austin, Judith Lytton, Olivia Meynell, Maurice Healy, Monica Saleeby, and Francis Meynell. Four early poems by Francis Thompson appear here for the first time in book form, by permission of his literary executor.

Contents open with Chesterton and Thompson pieces, including Threatened Tears, Arab Love Song, and Buona Notte. Colum's section follows, with An Idyll and Christ the Comrade among its poems. Readers get a snapshot of youthful verse of the 1910s, earnest and lyrical. The book suits readers of Georgian poetry.
18182-heralds-of-empire-being-the-story-:
A. C. Laut published this historical novel at Toronto in 1902. Its hero is Ramsay Stanhope, lieutenant to Pierre Radisson in the northern fur trade. Stanhope begins as a spoiled lad in his teens, taken by his nurse to Puritan kin in Boston after his father's death and a wasted family fortune. From there the story carries him into Radisson's world.

Chapters ask what king-killers are, tell of rescue and witchcraft, and follow Radisson's rivals, his game, and the white darkness of the north. Battles, inland peoples, and a bootless sacrifice mark the road to the end. Readers get the fur trade as adventure and as empire building, with Radisson's daring at its center and a young lieutenant learning its cost.
18873-contes-et-le-gendes-1re-partie:
H. A. Guerber, author of Myths of Greece and Rome, wrote this first part of Contes et Légendes for learners of French, published by the American Book Company in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago. The preface explains the method: stories told as simply as possible, with steady repetition of the same words and idioms, so pupils gain vocabulary almost without noticing.

The tales are chosen to stir curiosity and carry the reader to the end, avoiding the most familiar stories except for an opening Three Bears. Narration stays graphic and plain, suited to classroom reading. Readers get a gentle first reader in French, useful for beginners, and a sample of how language teaching worked before audio and graded readers.
19256-georgie:
Jacob Abbott wrote this 1857 Rollo story book about Georgie, a younger child who lives near Rollo under a hill by a stone bridge. A noble apple tree shades the small, pleasant house, and Georgie learns through play, money, friends, and a lecture on playthings. The book belongs to Abbott's moral series for children.

Georgie's mother explains that a plaything's worth lies not in itself but in the pleasure it wakes in the mind, using a baby with a stick as proof. Rollo and James listen and promise to remember. Young readers get a gentle lesson in thinking, sharing, and the wise use of toys.
20080-little-pollie:
Gertrude P. Dyer wrote Little Pollie, also called A Bunch of Violets, a tale for young readers. Pollie sells violets on the street, as the second title shows. Another girl asks how many she has sold that day. That girl is a London street child, tough from her earliest years.

Street girls in Victorian London faced cold, hunger, and hard bargaining daily. Yet the book finds hidden goodness beneath a rough surface. Pollie's tale blends pity, faith, and small acts of grace. Readers get a clear view of how such tales taught care for poor children.
20197-grandfather-s-love-pie:
Grandfather's Love Pie is a children's tale of family grief and comfort. A girl, Alsie, hears sorrow her grandfather did not mean to burden her with. He felt too sad to keep his grief shut in any longer. He had thought she was out playing with her friend Margaret.

Her mother, meanwhile, has gone to the drug store on an errand. Such small home details ground the tale in daily family life. Love pie, as the odd title hints, mixes sweetness with tears. Young readers get a tender story of old age, loss, and a child's care.
20355-vrouw-grobelaar-and-her-leading-ca:
Vrouw Grobelaar and Her Leading Cases, from 1906, holds seventeen short stories. Vrouw Grobelaar can spit Scripture at a person on small provocation. She bubbles with morality at almost every turn of talk. A mention of the accursed thing sets her effervescing with blame.

That phrase, she holds, covers half the goods of human commerce. Perceval Gibbon set these tales among the Boers of South Africa. The vrouw serves as a comic, formidable voice of her people. Readers get sharp, funny stories of farm, church, and veld life. Her voice, shrewd and funny, carries each short tale from start to end.
2039-evangeline-a-tale-of-acadie:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow tells in verse the fate of the Acadians, French settlers driven from their farms in Nova Scotia by the British. At the centre stands Evangeline, a young woman parted from her lover Gabriel on their wedding day. Longfellow wrote the poem in 1847, when American readers were eager for national legends of their own.

The poem follows her long search across America, from the forest primeval to distant settlements, as years pass and hope thins. Longfellow's steady, musical lines made the exile a national story, and Evangeline became a lasting symbol of faith kept through loss. The Acadian exile, called the Great Upheaval, gave him a true history on which to hang Evangeline's search.
20819-aims-and-aids-for-girls-and-young-:
Society, charges the Rev. G. S. Weaver, trains girls to be dolls and drudges. Aims and Aids for Girls and Young Women, from the 1850s, calls that training deplorably low. The best of society, Weaver insists, longs for something far better.

Duties of home, faith, work, and self-growth fill this earnest guide. Weaver urges girls to build minds and character, not mere fashion. His book counts among the bolder conduct guides of its day. It shows a reform strain in Victorian advice writing that pushed, within its limits, for women's fuller lives.
21122-more-about-pixie:
Pixie O'Shaughnessy returns in Mrs G. de Horne Vaizey's sequel, set at the end of the nineteenth century. The world of the books has electricity, telephones, trains, and buses, yet big households still depend on servants. Vaizey keeps Pixie's Irish warmth and bluntness at the centre of school and family life.

The sequel follows Pixie as she grows older among the friends and teachers readers met in Pixie O'Shaughnessy. Small scenes, like a butler finding a young couple kissing, show the author's comic touch. Feelings run true even where manners have dated. Several Pixie books followed, but this was the first return.
21980-motor-boat-boys-mississippi-cruise:
A motor boat race down the great river drives Louis Arundel's Motor Boat Boys Mississippi Cruise, published in 1914. Jack keeps his hand ready to reverse his engine at a second's warning on the frontispiece. The boys start for Dixieland and the Dixie Cup, meeting a handicap at the first station and peril soon after. Pudding, whose word is his strongest hold next to eating, serves as a boat-mate.

Bank robbers have their tables turned in a Kentucky cove, and the Wireless is taken in tow. Castaways in a swamp, a starving Buster, and the sheriff's posse crowd the run south. Arundel writes series adventure at full throttle. The river itself, from Kentucky to the land of cotton, is the real prize of the cruise.
22272-young-mr-barter-s-repentance-from-:
Young Mr. Barter's Repentance is one of the linked tales in David Christie Murray's Schwartz. It opens in the old offices of Bommaney, Waite, and Co. Mr. Bommaney is a British merchant of the highest rectitude and spotless reputation. He still trades under the firm's name, though Waite is long dead and the company vanished in his father's time.

Against that monument of respectability Murray sets young Barter, whose business character hides a private life. To see him on a certain April afternoon in 1880 would have shocked any of his friends. The tale works toward the repentance of its title. Murray enjoyed such contrasts of ledger and soul.
22904-i-ve-married-marjorie:
Margaret Widdemer's 1920 novel I've Married Marjorie opens on a bright New York morning. Mid-morning sidewalks belong to the middle-aged. Younger New Yorkers, Marjorie notes, are shut inside offices at ten or hurrying past in cars. Marjorie likes what she sees and breathes the spring air deeply. Then a black shadow crosses her pleasure.

That shadow drives a marriage story with more weight than its title suggests. Widdemer, a poet as well as a novelist, writes about a wife weighing love, duty, and a husband changed by war. The period detail is crisp, from office hours to motor cars. The book offers period romance with a serious undertow.
23102-this-world-must-die:
A hard-eyed woman boards in This World Must Die. Lipstick and a kinder hand with her cropped, ash-blonde hair might have made her pretty, the narrator judges. Her hard, suspicious stare sends his eyes down anyway. She crosses to the bulkhead and sits apart from the little group.

A spaceship's passenger cabin and a title like a sentence of doom set the story's terms. Strangers sized up in a waiting room will soon depend on one another, or fail to. The telling stays close and visual, letting faces carry foreshadowing. Readers get a taut piece of space fiction in the classic manner, where the end of a world begins with people watching each other warily.
23125-the-love-affairs-of-pixie:
Pixie O'Shaughnessy faces the mirror in The Love Affairs of Pixie. Pixie's twentieth birthday brings a shock. She is not beautiful, and suddenly she knows it. Family love and her own happy self-satisfaction had hidden the mirror's plain verdict from her until that day. Now her eyes stand open.

Mrs. George de Horne Vaizey's Pixie had already charmed readers in earlier books, and her love affairs test that charm where it counts. Plain looks and a rich spirit make the heroine's market value the joke and the question. Vaizey writes courtship with a clear eye for family comedy. Pixie's twentieth year keeps the series' warmth while letting its heroine grow up.
2370-sir-gibbie:
George MacDonald's Sir Gibbie follows a mute, homeless boy in a Scottish town who lives by kindness and instinct, speaking in actions where others use words. Gibbie's wanderings take him from a cruel household to the hills, where shepherds, lairds, and ministers test his goodness. MacDonald writes much of the dialogue in Broad Scots, with a glossary to help.

The novel is a spiritual romance about innocence and grace, earnest and deeply felt. Gibbie's silence makes him a mirror for everyone he meets. Readers of Victorian Scottish fiction will find a strange, moving book.
23952-valerie:
Captain Marryat's Valerie was the last book he worked on in his final days. It is unusual for him: a story of a lady's life, where he normally wrote the rough-and-tumble of shipboard life. Marryat had planned it from memoranda of a Frenchwoman's early life, up to seventeen, when she is left alone in the world, and wrote of it as Mademoiselle Virginie.

A preface letter of August 10, 1845, to Mrs. S. shows the book's conception, and another hand, perhaps Marryat's wife, completed it. Its episodes include young Lionel, raised from a junior servant to regain an estate rightfully his. The last chapters carry much reported speech, but the story rewards patience: a woman's life, told by a sailor who knew how to spin a yarn.
24000-miss-mackenzie:
Anthony Trollope published Miss Mackenzie in book form in 1865. Its heroine's father came from Scotland to London young and worked for his country all his life. He entered Somerset House as a clerk at sixteen and died still a clerk there.

Miss Mackenzie's career takes her to Littlebath, to the Cedars, and through a round of acquaintances, dinner parties, and philosophy. Mrs. Stumfold interferes, Mr. Maguire courts her, and the chapters show how two of her lovers behaved, then how the third behaved. A lion and a lamb, a Negro soldiers' orphan bazaar, and a wasp's sting on the lion. They fill out Trollope's comedy of a woman with money, suitors, and a mind of her own.
24443-an-australian-lassie:
Lilian Turner wrote this girls' story, published by Ward, Lock in London and Melbourne with illustrations by A. J. Johnson. It follows schoolgirl life at Wygate School, where a class list opens the book, and follows its heroine through pearl seeking, ghosts, a fight, and the daily round of lessons and friendships.

Later chapters take the girls from school to the city, with a note on a pincushion, a shilling, and a bent-shouldered old gentleman among the small mysteries along the way. The story is warm and episodic, giving young readers a charming picture of Australian schoolgirl life in the early twentieth century.
25695-the-diamond-coterie:
Lawrence L. Lynch, author of Shadowed by Three and Madeline Payne, writes this new detective story, The Diamond Coterie, published in Chicago by Sumner in 1884 with copyrights from 1882 and 1884. A sad affair, a character remarks in a front picture.

Two shocks for W open the plot, with W investigating, a sample of Lamotte blood, and Sybil's letter following. Deductions of a detective, Doctor Heath at home, and a falling out lead to one detective too many. Evan, the end of the beginning, and the beginning of the end carry a diamond mystery through Constance's diplomacy.
26057-marjorie:
Justin Huntly McCarthy's novel follows Marjorie through a chain of seafaring mishaps and island scenes. Lancelot Amber meets her near an alehouse by the river, and Captain Marmaduke's plan soon pulls the company aboard the Royal Christopher. Shipwreck divides the rough crew, and Marjorie bears the disaster with a calm that steadies those around her.

Later chapters move the party by raft to an island, where a feast, a discovery, and the loss of Cornelys Jensen test the group again. Marjorie stays the center of the tale, admired for her looks and her temper, while Lancelot's story is told in apology and retrospect. The book mixes romance, sea adventure, and a light utopian turn on the island.
2606-the-pigeon-pie:
Charlotte M. Yonge, author of The Heir of Redclyffe, wrote this historical tale, issued in a new edition by Mowbray in 1905. The title points to a homely dish with a secret purpose, and the story winds through families, loyalties, and dangers of an older England.

Yonge's young people must choose between safety and duty, while elders guard secrets that could ruin them. Her style is earnest and domestic, full of moral seriousness and affection for her characters. The book offers a gentle adventure for readers who like history told through household life.
26125-hoodie:
Mrs. Molesworth's Hoodie follows a small girl at war with the world, who sets out in search of a grandmother. Chapters carry her through a little baby and its mother, Maudie's godmother, stories told aloud, the chintz curtains, two trues, a foundling, a golden cage, and a flight. The tale ends with disobedience and waking.

At table, Martin scolds Hec and Hoodie for spilling food, warning that it forms a habit for later life, while Hoodie notes that Mr. Fielding once poured wine down the outside of her mother's glass. The book's charm lies in Hoodie's plain speech, her basket and big dog, and her cool view of grown-up faults.
26332-a-prize-for-edie:
J. F. Bone's short science-fiction story A Prize for Edie, illustrated by Schoenherr, opens with a Nobel Committee in trouble. The committee, the tag line says, made a mistake: Edie had indeed achieved the long-sought cancer cure, yet awarding her the Nobel Prize was still an error. A letter from America arrived too late, since acceptance had been taken as certain.

Since Pasternak, no Nobel laureate had refused the prize, so Professor Doctor Nels Christianson opened the letter without fear. His fellow committeemen, Dr. Eric Carlstrom and Dr. Sven Eklund, watched his face change as he read. The story builds its comedy from a prize that cannot be given as planned, and a committee with its neck out.
27342-athalie:
Robert W. Chambers published this novel with D. Appleton in New York and London in 1915, with illustrations by Frank Craig, and dedicated it to his friend Messmore Kendall. Its title figure is Athalie Greensleeve, and the story moves between country summers and city suppers, following Athalie, Clive, and C. Bailey Jr. through meetings, letters, and encounters.

Illustrations catch the novel's flavor: a boy asking to come down for the summer vacation and a supper at the Regina. They also show a stormy midnight meeting between Clive and Cecil Reeve, and a lovely May morning spent writing to Clive. Chambers writes the society romance of his period with ease and color. Readers of early twentieth-century popular fiction will find a lively, well-illustrated example.
28651-our-bessie:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's Our Bessie, published by the Mershon Company of Rahway and New York, opens with Bessie Lambert snowed up on a train. Nearly at journey's end, within sight and sound of home fires, she sits in an empty second-class compartment on a cold afternoon. Bessie, a cheerful optimist with pluck and quiet humor, treats the snowdrift as an adventure.

Later chapters introduce Hatty, the Kentish lanes, the Grange, Richard Sefton, and Bill Sykes. Edna's grievance, a first Sunday at the Grange, Bessie's second flitting, and a Japanese fan follow. Readers get a warm domestic novel about a good-natured girl and her circle.
28717-wee-wifie:
Rosa Nouchette Carey wrote this novel about a young wife nicknamed Wee Wifie, reissued in a cheaper, revised form after its first success. Carey added several fresh chapters to develop the story more fully, while leaving the characters and the main points of the plot untouched. The book opens with a prologue called The Wanderer, on a sunny autumn road by the sea.

Its heroine is a woman, tall and grave, with serious eyes and a sad, beautiful face, a woman who has suffered and been patient. The novel follows her marriage, her sorrows, and her endurance in the domestic style Carey made popular. Readers of Victorian family fiction get a sentimental but sincere tale of love, patience, and a wife's quiet strength.
28870-the-cabin-on-the-prairie:
Dr. C. H. Pearson wrote this frontier story, entered for copyright in 1869 and published by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard of Boston. Pearson dedicates it to his sister, whose spirit, he writes, has gone from prairie life to the hills of paradise. The book opens with a brawny pioneer from Maine, twenty years on the prairie, who warns the author that he will become so westernized he will lose his love for New England.

The story that follows mixes the author's own prairie memories with frontier incident: a capture of a fawn, a clay-stick-and-stone fireplace, and settlers' talk of old days. Pearson writes with affection for both East and West, and for the pioneer's generous heart. Readers get a gentle nineteenth-century portrait of prairie settlement, told by a man who lived it and missed New England still.
29160-operation-lorelie:
William P. Salton wrote this short science fiction story about war in a ruined future city. Two men in bulky protective suits pick their way through rubble, speaking by radio as if they were in deep space, and test the air before removing their helmets. The city around them is a wreck of what was once a great place.

Salton frames the tale with the old myth of Ulysses and the sirens, whose song lured sailors to ruin. In this new war of complete annihilation, some dangers stay the same, and a smiling voice can still be a weapon. Readers get a compact, grim story about soldiers who must guard against a lure as deadly as any bomb.
29173-the-white-lie:
William Le Queux published this spy and mystery novel in London in 1915. Its chapters promise a torn card, secrets of state, safe breakers, a downward path, and a grim truth, with a pretty stranger at the center of the opening mystery. Jean, the young woman at the story's heart, learns truths piece by piece as the plot tightens.

Later chapters bring Lord Bracondale's confession, sisters in silence, and a garden of love, mixing romance with espionage. Le Queux, a popular writer of spy tales, keeps the pace brisk and the secrets piling up. Readers get a wartime-era thriller about hidden papers, divided loyalties, and a lie told to protect someone, which grows harder to sustain with every chapter.
29319-the-trimming-of-goosie:
James Hopper published this novel in New York in 1909 with Moffat, Yard and Company, copyrighted by the Curtis Publishing Company. Its hero, Goosie, is otherwise Mr. Charles Norton Sims, and the book's dedication names Mrs. Charles Norton Sims. Chapter one finds Goosie caught between a porcelain tub and a gleaming towel-rack, performing morning calisthenics before a mirror.

Goosie drops his arms, stands very still, and blushes at his own reflection, panic bounding between man and mirror. Hopper, author of Caybigan and 9009, writes comedy from embarrassment and self-regard. Readers get a humorous novel of manners about a man being trimmed, in every sense, by the world around him.
29735-martians-never-die:
Lucius Daniel builds this short tale on a yearly wait. A young reporter walks into a circular brick building at three-fifteen to ask about Dr. Clyde Curtis. Stern, hard-eyed, greets him as a cub, though the reporter has been on the paper a whole year. Beryl Curtis, the doctor's wife, joins the talk.

Curtis is lost, stuck, or dead, by common guess, after trusting stellar currents that even Einstein cannot work out. Beryl says the trip back to Earth is open only once a year, when those currents permit it. The epigraph promises a strange bodyguard: no bark, no bite, no sting, just conversion of the enemy. The tale turns on that wait and its strange end.
29947-spacemen-never-die:
Morris Hershman wrote Spacemen Never Die. Its headnote frames its trouble: Henry knew his wife had been married once before. Now he expected her to start a new life with him, but to her the past was alive. Henry Weller stands facing a huge three-dimensional picture on his dining room wall and asks his wife if they can get rid of it.

Phoebe shakes her blonde head and refuses. Don Manton loved her and was famous, she says, and she likes recalling days when her picture filled the telepapers and her face filled telescreens. Henry, a foreman in a humandroid factory, is stopped from answering by Phoebe leaving for a bit of shopping. He watches her takeoff from their two-story fibroid house, then takes the picture down by its luminex frame, stubborn to the core.
30497-the-foreign-hand-tie:
David Gordon writes a science fiction story from Analog, December 1961, about the limits of seeing and of telepathy. Its tagline warns that seeing a thing does not mean understanding it, and that even perfect telepathy may fail as communication.

The tale opens with a geography lesson: Istanbul in Turkish Thrace to Moscow is under eleven hundred miles in a beeline, a couple of hours by fast jet. Mr. Raphael Poe, however, has no way to charter a bee, while the cruiser Woonsocket sails the Mediterranean, Aegean, and Dardanelles to Istanbul and back. Gordon uses travel and telepathy to test how minds truly meet.
30941-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
Held here is volume nineteen of The German Classics of the Nineteenth and Twentieth Centuries, masterpieces of German literature translated into English. It was published by the German Publication Society in New York in 1914. Kuno Francke of Harvard served as editor-in-chief, with William Guild Howard as assistant editor, and the set ran to twenty illustrated volumes. This volume gathers the contemporary short story.

Its writers include Helene Böhlau, Clara Viebig, Eduard von Keyserling, Thomas Mann, Ludwig Thoma, Rudolf Hans Bartsch, Emil Strauss, Hermann Hesse, Ernst Zahn, and Jakob Schaffner. Translators include Bayard Quincy Morgan, for Gay Hearts, Tonio Kröger, Matt the Holy, and The Styrian Wine-Carter, and Howard, for Burning Love and Mara. It is a rich sampler of German fiction at the turn of the century, in English dress.
31334-descriptions-of-two-species-of-fro:
William E. Duellman's 1961 paper, fifth in his Studies of American Hylid Frogs, describes two new species of the genus Ptychohyla from field work in southern Mexico and northern Central America. Taylor had proposed the genus in 1944 for a frog from Agua del Obispo, Guerrero, defining it by large ventrolateral glands and horny nuptial spines in breeding males.

Stuart later noted both traits are seasonal, and described a species lacking the spines, while Duellman found two groups of species separated by four characters, both with large glands in breeding males. Published as volume 13, number 8 of the Kansas museum series, the paper adds two names to a genus long poorly represented in museums.
32619-back-to-julie:
Richard Wilson's Back to Julie, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in May 1954, turns on the side-shuffle, a way of stepping sideways between dimensions. Its narrator is one of the rare people functionally equipped for the trip. He bargains hard with Krasnow, a crooked district attorney who wants to be governor and then president.

The narrator must travel naked, without so much as a sandal or a tooth filling, and takes ten percent in cash in advance. Krasnow needs the people, and the narrator, who has visited the farthest branch of the time-tree, can give him what he wants, at a price paid in any coin.
32683-the-next-time-we-die:
Robert Moore Williams sets this tale in a wild desert, where Nora Martin, an archaeologist, and Pike McLean, a roustabout, lie low from native fighters. Nora wonders why they left Earth homes and families for such a place, while McLean takes death lightly, as a hired hand takes hard work.

McLean claims he has died hundreds of times, since life first crawled from mud flats and left its gills behind. Rebirth, he says, is how humankind takes another crack at the puzzle of growth, until one day it may inherit the farther stars. The tale asks whether ideals are worth dying for, and what the next death may teach.
32802-tillie:
Craig Browning tells of Tillie, a blob of living metal with emotions like any woman's, in this story from Amazing Stories of December 1948. Bill Halley, a physics professor nicknamed Comet, watches his chief Judson Taylor pull a bright silver lump, shaped like a pocket knife, from his pocket.

The lump is warm, too light for a heavy element, and settles slowly without a bounce. Biochemist Mallory made it by accident from spilled chemicals and a rare enzyme. Taylor finds he can make it weigh a ton by looking at it hard, then light again. Tillie, too, wants romance, and is not coy about running after her guy, even aboard a ship where gravity pulls bodies at odd angles.
32959-leerie:
Ruth Sawyer's Leerie, copyrighted in 1920, gathers stories around lamplighters, the men who once walked city streets at dusk with ladder and light. Sawyer dedicates the book to lamplighters the world over, and her tales move from a man who feared sleep to Old King Cole, a changeling, and a lad who outsang the stars. Each story catches a small, strange moment when the ordinary world tilts toward wonder.

The title comes from the old cry for the lamplighter, and Sawyer treats her figures with warmth rather than irony. Her prose is gentle and musical, suited to reading aloud, and the book's afterword closes a circle begun in its foreword. It is a collection for readers who like folklore's quiet magic, where kindness and a lit lamp can stand against the dark.
34003-left-on-the-prairie:
M. B. Cox, writing as Noel West, wrote this boys' prairie tale, published in London in 1899 with pictures by A. Pearce. Little Jack Wilson, born in England, lives at Longview and soon finds trouble, a resolution, and a journey. Chapters follow Jack deserted on the prairie, Jack rescued, and what Jack learned from Pedro.

Jack arrives at Swift Creek Ranch, visits there, and crosses the range with Champion Joe, until at last he finds his mother. A frontispiece shows a terrible fight between a man and a horse. The book offers a stirring tale of a boy alone on the prairie.
34436-hints-to-husbands-a-revelation-of-:
George Morant, late of the Grenadier Guards, wrote Hints to Husbands, a revelation of the man-midwife's mysteries, in a third edition printed in London in 1857. Morant dedicates the book to the husbands and fathers of the United Kingdom. He also addresses those medical men who condemn man-midwifery as an outrage on the modesty of women.

His preface states a two-fold object: to expose and amend a vast social evil. To bring the evil before public opinion, he says, he must probe it to the core and drag its indecent mysteries into the light. He expects censure from easy-going people who hold that ignorance is bliss. The book belongs to a long Victorian quarrel over who should attend women in childbirth, argued here with a soldier's bluntness and a moralist's heat.
35475-songs-of-the-prairie:
Songs of the Prairie, a book of poems by Robert Stead, was published in New York in 1912. Stead was already known for Prairie Born, an earlier verse book. The contents list more than thirty poems, from The Plow and The Homesteader to The Canadian Rockies and Who Owns the Land?

The title poem sets city against prairie and calls the prairie the mother of all. The city, in Stead's lines, fawns on the rich and clever, while the open land stays broad, clean, and true. Other poems treat mothers, gramophones, hard work in jeans, and going home. Plain rhymes and strong local pride mark the whole set, written for prairie settlers and their kin.
35757-our-katie:
A tract tells a child's life in Our Katie, published by the American Tract Society of New York. A plate carries a verse on her: she taught us how to live, and, too high the price of knowledge, taught us how to die. The tale is told as fact, for young readers.

Katie was born in Ireland, the tale starts. At an early age her parents emigrated to this country and settled in Brooklyn. She was one of a family of ten children, several older than herself. Yet from her earliest childhood she appeared to be a ruling spirit among them. Naturally quick and apt to learn, she readily adapted herself to the manners of the new people. Katie was not beautiful, nor even pretty, the tale owns. But there was an earnest look in her large dark eyes, and her amiable disposition endeared her to everyone.
36612-the-princess-and-curdie:
The Princess and Curdie is George MacDonald's fairy tale of the miner boy Curdie, issued by J B Lippincott and Company of Philadelphia in 1883. James Allen supplied eleven illustrations. The title page gives the author his doctor's degree, and the tale stands among his best-loved books for children.

The chapters open on the mountain and a white pigeon, then bring Curdie before the Mistress of the Silver Moon. She gives him his mission, and the gift bound up with hands: by touch he learns what a man is becoming within. The strange creature Lina joins him, and more creatures follow on the heath. MacDonald opens the tale by telling how stones are pieces of the heart of the earth, escaped from the dungeon below.
3756-indiscretions-of-archie:
P G Wodehouse sends his amiable Englishman Archie to America, where he falls in love with Lucille, daughter of a millionaire hotel keeper, and marries her on the spot. From Archie's view the match is a thoroughly good egg, but his father-in-law, Mr Brewster, thinks otherwise, since Archie has neither money nor occupation. The comedy that follows is a duel between Archie's cheerful blundering and Brewster's glares.

Chapters pile up the mishaps, from an artist's model and a bomb to a sausage chappie, a missing pair of pyjamas, and a night of worry on a pine scented balcony. Wodehouse keeps the tone light and the dialogue brisk. Readers who like farce with manners will find Archie a hero who wins by luck, charm, and total refusal to take alarm.
37838-the-story-of-louie:
The Story of Louie is a novel by Oliver Onions, printed in New York by George H Doran Company. Onions had written In Accordance with the Evidence and the Debit Account. He gives the book to Gwladys. A prologue opens the tale, then five parts.

The parts are named Rainham Parva, Sutherland Place, Mortlake Road, Pillar to Post, and the Consolidation. An envoi closes the book. The prologue opens in an old number of Punch, under the heading Society New Pet, the Artist Model. A drawing by Du Maurier shows a duchess asking Miss Dragon how she and Mr Sopley came to quarrel. Miss Dragon answers that she was sitting to him in a cestus for the Judgment of Paris when someone called. Novel fans get a model life across London addresses.
39093-life-of-beethoven-including-his-co:
Ignace Moscheles edited this life of Beethoven, published by Henry Colburn in London in 1841 in two volumes. The file holds volume one. The book rests on Schindler's biography of the composer, translated into English. Moscheles, a pianist, added notes, traits, and letters to complete the picture. His preface explains his share in the work and the care he felt it demanded.

Alongside the life, the volume prints Beethoven's correspondence with his friends. It also gathers remarks on his musical works and stories that show his character. Moscheles writes that the subject called for seriousness and reverence. The result is an early English life of the composer, built from a close friend's account and enriched by a fellow musician who knew the world Beethoven moved in.
40192-a-student-s-history-of-england-v-2:
Publisher pages for Samuel Rawson Gardiner's many histories open the hosted text. They list his History of England in ten volumes, his Great Civil War in four, and A Student's History of England in three. Then the title page of volume two appears. Longmans, Green issued the reissue at London and New York in nineteen fourteen, a new impression of the nineteen two edition. The volume runs from fifteen nine to sixteen eighty nine.

The contents open with part five, The Renascence and the Reformation, dated fifteen nine to sixteen three. Its first chapter treats Henry VIII. The series places this volume between a first volume from the earliest times to fifteen nine and a third running to nineteen ten. Students get a school history of Tudor and Stuart England by a leading historian of the age.
4025-anna-christie:
Eugene O'Neill's play in four acts follows Anna Christopherson, daughter of Chris, captain of the coal barge Simeon Winthrop. In a waterfront bar, Chris orders wine for Anna and small beer for himself, pleased to say she is reforming him already.

Anna arrives tired and guarded, drying her eyes and trying to smile as her father pats her hand. O'Neill sets the play among longshoremen, bartenders, and stokers such as Mat Burke, where sea fog and old sins hang over new hope. The play won wide praise for its blunt, tender portrait of a father and daughter seeking a fresh start.
40611-prince-charlie:
Burford Delannoy, the author of The Margate Mystery, sets this novel in Wivernsea, a small seaside resort not yet developed enough for a regatta, as the opening jokes. Fenno and Company of New York published it, with a frontispiece. Lodging house keepers watch the season end and the visitors scuttle away as September turns.

The contents promise a love story worked through misunderstandings. Hero and heroine meet, a danger signal sounds, and a voice speaks in the darkness. Feverish symptoms, white lies, and a horrible revelation follow. Dick's good temper is lost and resumed, a teacup storm blows through, and the book ends where such novels end, at Christmas Eve and the Christmas box. Delannoy wrote fiction for the holiday and railway trade, and this one keeps its seaside town, its courtship, and its reconciliations all in the key of gentle comedy.
41608-drum-taps-in-dixie:
Drum Taps in Dixie, by Delavan Miller, holds the memories of a drummer boy of 1861 to 1865. The Hungerford-Holbrook company printed it at Watertown, New York, in December 1905. Miller gives the book to his wife and children, and a portrait fronts it.

A prelude lets the drum speak first, an odd stroke. The old drum tells of twisted leather ears, scratched sides, and a patched, blood-stained head. It led men on the march and in battle, and now rests in a cosy attic corner. The first chapter opens with the news that Fort Sumter had been fired on. The writer was a boy of twelve, living at West Carthage. Flags went up on churches, schools, shops, and poor homes alike. Boys drilled in the streets, and fought mock battles on Saturdays.
41691-darkey-ways-in-dixie:
Margaret Richard wrote the poems collected as Darkey Ways in Dixie, published by the Abbey Press in New York in 1901. The book presents verse in a written dialect meant to copy the speech of Black people in the South of that day. A Charleston ground-nut woman appears in the frontispiece.

The pieces take up washerwomen, hucksters, well-cleaners, and boot-blacks at their work. Others treat Christmas gifts, blackberry time, church meetings, weddings, and funerals. One poem honors Booker T. Washington, and several turn on jokes, superstition, and hard luck. Modern readers will find the book a period piece. It shows how white writers of 1901 packaged Black life for white audiences. Its dialect style is now read as a record of its time.
41760-the-poetical-works-of-james-beatti:
Little, Brown of Boston published the poems of James Beattie in 1854, with a life of the author by Alexander Dyce. Beattie was born on October 25, 1735, at Laurencekirk in Scotland. His father kept a small shop and rented a little farm. The boy was the youngest of six children and lost his father at the age of seven.

The chief poem in the book is The Minstrel, a tale of the progress of genius in two books. Shorter pieces include Retirement, an elegy, and an ode to hope. A set of poems that Beattie himself cut from later editions stands in a part of its own. The book also holds his versions of Horace, Virgil, Lucretius, and Anacreon. Epitaphs close the list, one among them meant for the poet himself. Dyce's life gives the facts with care and warmth.
42408-growing-up-a-story-of-the-girlhood:
Growing Up is a tale of the girlhood of Judith Mackenzie by Jennie Drinkwater. A verse on years grown sacred heads the front page of the book. Rights date the work to the year eighteen ninety four. The tale aims at girls who stand where Judith stands in her youth.

Parts treat a horn book, sums, a home named Bensalem, and daily bread. A small convert, a key tale, and a turn point mark the mid course of her years. Aunt Affy gives faith talks and walks with the girl through doubt and choice. Talks on women and a far letter close the long list of her days. Faith, home, and growth in grace form the spine of the tale.
42426-gold-elsie:
Gold Elsie, a novel from the German of E Marlitt, was translated by Mrs A L Wister and published by J B Lippincott and Company of Philadelphia in 1868. Marlitt was the pen name of a German writer whose tales of proud heroines and old houses pleased readers on two continents. The Old Mam'selle's Secret, named on the title page, had already made her name in America.

Snow has fallen all day as the first chapter opens. Twilight brings a wild gust among the flakes over the capital, and the gas lamps take the place of the stars. Carriages whirl round the corners, and flower crowned heads peep from behind the glass. Wax heads stare from the warm shop windows, and old flower sellers stand among their blooms. In that bright, cold crowd the story of Elsie begins, the golden hearted girl of the title.
45032-the-principal-species-of-wood-thei:
Charles Henry Snow wrote a plain guide to the main kinds of wood and their traits. John Wiley and Sons issued the first form in New York in 1903. Snow led the School of Applied Science at New York University. A live oak of Louisiana fronts the illustrated book.

Snow says past works stressed strength or served deep experts alone. He writes for builders and users who need to tell woods apart in practice. Notes draw on the United States Division of Forestry and on trade journals. Grain, weight, color, and use mark each kind in a book made for shop and office.
45108-p-t-barnum-s-menagerie:
Barnum's Menagerie is a picture book of wild animals for little people. Barnum and Sarah Burke arranged its text and illustrations together. White and Allen published it in New York and London in 1888. Strobridge Lithographing gave aid the publishers praise on the front pages. Coloured plates show the beasts in their cages for young eyes.

With the Animals opens with a warm address to dear children in print. Unless a grown up friend took them, Barnum says, much stays hidden. That friend would answer all their questions at the cages with patience. He would tell all about the bewitchingly horrible animals inside them. The showman's voice turns a cage row into a guided tour.
45788-the-german-classics-of-the-ninetee:
The German Classics is a twenty-volume set of masterpieces of German literature in English translation. This text is volume eleven, copyrighted in 1914 by the German Publication Society of New York. The volume holds works by Friedrich Spielhagen, Theodor Storm, and Wilhelm Raabe. A painting of the North Sea coast fronts the book.

Professors of German at American universities wrote the lives of the three authors. Translators include Marion Learned, who renders Storm's Storm Flood, and Muriel Almon, who translates The Rider of the White Horse and The Hunger Pastor. The Patrons' Edition was sold to spread German letters in America on the eve of the First World War.
46608-shall-turkey-live-or-die:
Shall Turkey Live or Die?, by Thomas Carlyle, an advocate, was printed in London in 1854, as war over the East loomed. The pamphlet opens by saying the coming European war differs from the last in its ground, its origin, and its stakes. No contest, it claims, rose in more mystery or was less welcome to those who must fight it.

Three sorts of men watch the crisis: prophets who read it as Scripture fulfilled, planners who draw new maps, and practical men who press old duties. The writer warns against mapping the future by pride and against judging events by the mere letter of treaties. Destiny is the watchword, he says, as the Crescent's horn rests on Christendom.
48444-a-modern-aladdin-or-the-wonderful-:
A Modern Aladdin is a play by Howard Pyle, published by Harper and Brothers of New York in 1892. Its full title names it the wonderful adventures of Oliver Munier. The piece is billed as an extravaganza in four acts. Pyle drew the pictures as well as writ the play. The frontispiece shows a dull heavy smoke rising to a ceiling. The plate list names the Count de St Germaine as a chief of the tale. A strange gentleman in black, who claims to be Oliver's uncle, stands near the start.

The scenes run through lighted matches in vases, gems spread on a table, and dances of a grotesque kind. Mademoiselle Céleste and a marquis fill out the cast. Pyle retells the lamp tale as a stage romp of magic and wealth. It is the Arabian tale in modern dress, made for the eye.
49405-trial-of-deacon-brodie:
William Roughead put in shape the trial tale of Deacon Brodie of Edinburgh. The book came out in 1906 in the Notable Scottish Trials set. It is given, by leave, to Lord Dundas in fond terms. A front plate shows Brodie's first meet with George Smith. That meet was drawn from an old print by Kay.

Brodie was a town chief by day and a house thief by night. Roughead built his tale from the true court file, he says. Town prints and hand notes of that day fill the gaps. No full life of Brodie had been tried till then, he notes. Crime past fans get a strange, true tale in full.
50412-the-americans-in-the-great-war-v-2:
The Americans in the Great War, volume two, is part of the Michelin Illustrated Guides to the Battlefields of 1914 to 1918. Michelin and Company of Clermont-Ferrand issued the guides in French and English editions for visitors to the war ground. This volume covers the Battle of Saint Mihiel, with St Mihiel, Pont-à-Mousson, and Metz.

The guide teaches the tourist to read the battlefield as he would read a town from its street plan, using Michelin maps at a clear scale. Its front matter praises the Michelin wheel, detachable at the hub by six bolts and proven on all fronts. These guides let veterans and families retrace the American fight in the Saint Mihiel salient, road by road and village by village.
5267-sister-carrie:
Theodore Dreiser's Sister Carrie follows Caroline Meeber, a young woman who leaves her Wisconsin home for Chicago in search of a better life. Working in a shoe factory and drawn to the theatre, Carrie meets the travelling salesman Drouet. Later she meets the saloon manager Hurstwood, whose love carries her to New York and the stage.

Dreiser writes of desire, money, and the city with a frankness that shocked his first publishers. The novel became a landmark of American naturalism. Readers will find a heroine who rises as Hurstwood falls. Success and ruin trade places in that portrait of American ambition.
53039-the-world-s-earliest-music-traced-:
Hermann Smith traced the first music of man through old lands and relics. Sixty-five plates aid his book of finds and tools. A marble Apollo with his lyre fronts the work. Smith wrote on the organ and on band tools as well. An Arab saw heads it: the eye is blind when the mind can not see.

Greece, Etruria, Egypt, and China give their proof in turn. Assyria and Babylon lead back to Akkad and Sumer, the first home. Pipes, harps, and bells in stone and bronze tell the tale. Smith weighs tale, file, and found thing side by side. Music past fans get a vast, rich dig.
53362-a-rebellion-in-dixie:
Harry Castlemon wrote A Rebellion in Dixie, a boys' tale of the Civil War South, published in Philadelphia by Coates and Company in 1897. Castlemon had made his name with the Gunboat Series, the Hunter Series, and the War Series, all named on the title page. A front picture shows men replacing a notice.

Nineteen chapters carry the home-front adventure. The tale turns to the work of war near home: capturing a wagon train, breaking a mule, and rebels in the rear. A night expedition and revenge by the rebels fill the middle. Leon falls prisoner, and Coleman proves his honesty before the close. The first words set the muster: Leon is to take in everybody and leave not a single man out. Boys of 1897 got the war at their own scale.
53610-a-sister-to-evangeline-being-the-s:
Charles G D Roberts wrote A Sister to Evangeline, the story of Yvonne de Lamourie and her exile with the villagers of Grand Pre. Lamson, Wolffe and Company published it at Boston in 1898. Roberts dedicated the book to his mother. Thirty-eight chapters fill it. Paul Grande's homecoming to Grand Pre opens the tale. Grul's warning, charms and counter-charms, and the Black Abbe follow.

Father Fafard, the ferry, and a Grand Pre morning fill the early chapters. Beauserjour and after, Grul's case, and the Lower Ford come midway. The chapel prison and the ships of her exile raise the close. The hour of her desolation and a woman's privilege precede the boarding of the Good Hope. The court in the cabin and sword and silk end the run.
53764-the-tower-menagerie:
The Tower Menagerie describes the animals kept at the Tower of London. Robert Jennings published it in London in 1829. Portraits of each animal were drawn from life by William Harvey. Branston and Wright engraved them on wood. The volume is dedicated, by permission, to King George the Fourth. He was patron of the royal menagerie the book describes.

An introduction traces menageries back to remote antiquity. The lion entries open the catalogue: Bengal, Cape, and Barbary kinds. Tiger, leopard, jaguar, and puma follow in order. Hyenas, wolves, jackals, and civets fill the middle pages. Bears of four kinds and many monkeys come next. The kangaroo, porcupine, and Asiatic elephant close the beasts. Eagles, vultures, the secretary bird, and macaws end the list. Anecdotes of each animal's character mix with natural history.
53911-short-title-catalog-of-publication:
Short-Title Catalog is a publisher's catalogue of scientific and engineering books, issued by Van Nostrand Company of New York in August 1910. The list covers the firm's own publications and its importations. The firm was sole American agent for several English technical publishers, among them Scott, Greenwood and Company, Constable, Crosby Lockwood, and the Electrician company.

The entries run alphabetically by author, with format and price. Abbott's work on the electrical transmission of energy stands at five dollars. A practical bookbinding manual, translated by Maw, is two and a half. Sewers and drains for populous districts, a practical book on X-ray work, and codes for telegraphy fill the first page. Catalogues like this one were the finding lists of the technical world: an engineer in Ohio ordered his shelf from these columns.
55143-the-story-of-the-mince-pie:
Josephine Scribner Gates wrote Christmas tales for children round a mince pie. The book came out in New York in 1916. John Rae drew the pictures. Gates thanks Mildred Potter for the thought of a pie as hero. Two of the tales first ran in Saint Nicholas magazine.

When the pie is cut, dolls step out to tell tales. Raisin Doll, Currant Doll, and Clove Doll each take a turn. A dance of the dolls and more tales fill the book. Song-like verse at the front toasts spice, fruit, and crust. Young readers get sweet tales for the feast days. The pie hides a world in its crust.
55335-the-mercer-boys-cruise-in-the-lass:
Capwell Wyckoff's The Mercer Boys' Cruise in the Lassie was published in 1948 by the World Publishing Company of Cleveland and New York, as a Falcon Book. The cover copy sends Don and Jim Mercer and their buddy Terry Mackson out in their sloop Lassie. Their goal is Mystery Island, and they go in search of fun.

What they find, the blurb promises, is more than they bargained for: real danger, a brush with marine bandits, and a fight for their lives. The contents run to stormy weather, an inner room, an old captain, and a boy blown out to sea. A red lamp, a river barge, the ghost of the Alaskan, and the Black Mummy keep the cruise moving to its end.
55666-the-german-spy-in-america-the-secr:
John Price Jones wrote The German Spy in America. Hutchinson and Company issued it at London in 1917. Its subtitle promises the inside story of the Lusitania's sinking. Theodore Roosevelt wrote words in its favor up front. Roger B Wood wrote the intro. Wood had served as a federal prosecutor in New York.

Roosevelt read the book's proofs in February 1917. He praised it with all emphasis, his letter says. Jones does the country a great service, he wrote. The facts rest on government records, Roosevelt claims. German agents used America as a war base, he charges. They waged war on American lives and goods, he adds. That war ran two and one half years by his count. A wartime expose named names from court files while America still debated entering the great war.
57848-the-essentials-of-good-skirmishing:
The Essentials of Good Skirmishing is a drill book for light troops by Gawler, late of a famed light foot band. This is its second form, put out at London in the mid eighteen hundreds from a war book house by the halls of rule. New parts crowd its title page.

A brief set of plain light drill is now bound in. A plan of drill for the swift gain of skill with the rifle joins it. Short notes on gear and dress that serve a man in the field close the adds. Its gift word makes it out to the chief clerk of the whole force of the land. Its aim is plain: how a loose line of men should scout, screen, and fight in front of the main host.
58241-library-essays-papers-related-to-t:
Arthur Bostwick wrote papers on the work of public book houses. His book came out in New York in 1920. The first paper, on pains in such work, dates to 1902. It was read at a meet of the American Library Association. More papers come from the Library Journal and like prints.

How book men choose books is the theme of one piece. The small town book house gets its own close look. Lay rule of book houses and a trustee's whole duty stand there. Bostwick's own chief's talk at Lake Placid ends the front set. Book folk get a pro's frank view of their trade. Plain talk rules each short piece.
58434-minkie:
Louis Tracy, who wrote The Wings of the Morning, set this tale of Africa in a short, sharp frame. McLeod and Allen printed Minkie at Toronto in 1907. Five long chapters carry the whole book, each with a plain, hard name.

How a Bogey-Man Came to Dale End opens it. Prince John's Strange Ally follows. Then come the paired heads: The White Man's Way and The Black Man's Way. The Undoing of Schwartz closes the list. Tracy's Africa is a place of posts, fevers, and armed pride, where two codes of honor grind against each other. Minkie herself stands in the title plate, the heart of the tale. A brisk yarn of its empire age.
58492-a-confession-of-evangelical-princi:
Church's A Confession of Evangelical Principles, in a letter to a friend, was printed and sold by Cheney at Banbury in 1808, price sixpence. Church was minister at Banbury in Oxfordshire; Cheney was printer to the Duke of Clarence. A text from Jude stands on the title page: earnestly contend for the faith once delivered to the saints.

The letter, dated Banbury, February 1, 1808, answers four charges. First, that he holds and propagates antinomian sentiments. Second, that he creates divisions wherever he preaches. Third, that those who come to hear him cannot afterwards hear their own ministers with pleasure. Fourth, that he does not preach to sinners. Heavy charges, he calls them. His confession declares his doctrines to be those of the Articles of the Church of England and the Westminster Confession of Faith. The Scriptures of both Testaments are his only rule of faith and practice.
58620-the-power-of-a-lie:
The Power of a Lie, by Johan Bojer, was turned from the Norwegian by Jessie Muir and printed by Heinemann at London in 1908. Hall Caine writes the first words, and the tale bears a crown from the French Academy. It opens on a dark lake in winter. Old Knut Norby drives his sledge home from a school board meet, though he vowed to his wife he would shun the thin ice. The day has galled him at each turn.

He lost a vote, his son-in-law begged a fresh loan on his birthright, and a merchant's fall left him bound for a great sum. He cracks the whip and takes the ice road all the same. Novel fans get a stern Norse study of pride, debt, and the first small crack in a man's truth.
58824-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Works of Barrie is a guide to the books of the famed Scots pen. That shelf stands free on the web. The guide was built by Widger as a path through those works. Its lists give each book and its parts in full.

The boy who would not grow up leads its list, in form on form. First come the tale with Wendy and the play. The tale in prints and the park tale twice told join them. A bird book of the same park and a mums praise book come next. A run of plays crowds the lines past them: a good butler, a plea for the old ways, and what each woman knows.
59457-seedtime-in-kashmir-a-memoir-of-wi:
