Seedtime in Kashmir is a memoir of William Jackson Elmslie, a doctor and church worker in Kashmir, written by his widow with his friend W Burns Thomson. The book was printed in London in 1875. Elmslie held degrees from Scotland and served with the Church Missionary Society.

Early chapters trace his school days, his time as a medical student in Aberdeen and Edinburgh, and his trip from Calcutta to Kashmir. Later parts cover road side work in Amritsar and his first and second years of work in Kashmir. The widow notes in the preface that she was in India and could not revise the book. Readers meet a young doctors life of faith, care, and hard travel in a far land.
6043-the-spanish-tragedie:
Thomas Kyd's Spanish Tragedie of 1587, in John Matthews Manly's 1897 edition, promises the lamentable end of Don Horatio and Bel-Imperia, with the pitiful death of old Hieronimo. Newly corrected from faults of the first impression and printed at London by Edward Allde for Edward White, it stands among the earliest English revenge tragedies.

The persons include the ghost of Andrea and Revenge itself, setting a frame where the dead demand justice. Manly's editor chose clearer readings over footnoted alternatives and left out insertions once ascribed to Ben Jonson, with alternate dialogue marked as such. Kyd's play mixes court, murder, and madness in high early modern verse.
60443-eddie:
Eddie is a science fiction tale by Frank Riley, printed in Worlds of If in December 1957. Its frame presents the case of John O'Hara Smith, a research man in electronics, as a landmark in the annals of spies and counterspies. The claim is bold: no one person did more to advance the methods of that secret trade.

For over a year the case was known to only a few men in security and defense posts. A few leaks reached the papers and were hotly denied. The tale then rebuilds the case from records since cleared and from two papers Smith gave to a research body, asking whether he was spy, counterspy, or dead.
60732-industries-and-inventions-of-the-s:
Two Canterbury sisters, Bertha Lindsay and Lillian Phelps, gave these talks on the industries, inventions, and music of the Shakers. The herb trade comes first, and it was no small thing. The Shakers, Eldress Anna White wrote, were first in this country to put roots, herbs, and vegetable extracts for medicine on the market. Thomas Corbett of Canterbury made the famous Syrup of Sarsaparilla and the Wild Cherry Pectoral Syrup.

The figures surprise. In 1848 the sisters cleaned and packaged 9,327 pounds of roots. In 1871 they put up 14,079 bottles of one tincture alone. In one year more than a million labels were cut. The physics gardens at Mount Lebanon covered over fifty acres, with some 200 varieties of native plants. Witch-hazel was still distilled at Canterbury in 1910. The talks preserve a communal economy from inside, with pride and exact numbers.
61946-jesse-james-desperate-game-or-the-:
Jesse James' Desperate Game is a dime novel by William Ward, one of the Adventure Series tales of western outlaws. Its sub-title names the deed at its heart: the robbery of the Ste Genevieve bank. With three companions only, the bandit steals ten thousand dollars. He then eludes a posse of detectives with dare-devil nerve. A note to the reader puffs the series as the true history of the James boys and their kind. The same house sold the life of Jesse James by his only son.

The first chapter, A Thrilling Rescue, opens at Monegaw Springs in Missouri. The town is a health resort in Saint Clair county, famed for its waters. After the civil war the country folk came back without fear of raids. Board was scarce, and late comers slept in tents. Into this scene the tale brings its bandit hero and his game.
63025-a-night-in-acadie:
A Night in Acadie, by Kate Chopin, author of Bayou Folk, was published in Chicago in 1897. Twenty-one short tales of Louisiana make up the book, starting with the title tale. Names such as Athenaise, Polydore, Caline, Azelie, and Mamouche mark the French and Creole world of the bayou country.

Other tales treat regret, prejudice, ripe figs, and a respectable woman. Chopin writes of love, duty, faith, and small-town watchfulness in a spare, keen prose. Settings run from farms and bayous to the shore at Cheniere Caminada. The tales show Chopin at her sharpest on women's inner lives and the tight rules of Acadie society, two years before her famed novel.
6315-the-awakening-of-helena-richie:
Dr. Lavendar and his horse Goliath toil up a hill to call on old Benjamin Wright, then jog back in late afternoon with the complacency that follows a disagreeable duty done. Rain has turned clay to stiff mud, Goliath dislikes the climb, and the doctor dislikes the call, yet he tells his small old dog Daniel that likings do not govern pastoral visits. By the road stands the Stuffed Animal House, named for a taxidermist owner, a visit deferred to next week.

Margaret Deland's novel, dated May 12, 1906, centres on Helena Richie, whose awakening unfolds in the village world of Old Chester, with Dr. Lavendar, Mary, and little David at its heart. David's bedtime blessings, taught by the doctor, bless everybody from Goliath to Mrs. Richie. Deland writes village life with warmth and moral care, as a woman's conscience wakes to love, duty, and the claims of a child.
64122-the-story-of-a-pumpkin-pie:
William Barton told this children's story in verses, and Willard told it in pictures, in a book published by the Pilgrim Press of Boston and Chicago under an 1898 copyright. The publisher's preface explains that just before Christmas 1897, Willard sent his friend Barton twenty pencil sketches showing the evolution of a pumpkin pie. Barton wrote verses to go with them for his own children.

Willard was famous as the painter of Yankee Doodle and of Pluck, a pair of pictures of children in a homemade cart drawn by a dog. The verses begin in spring, when Carl, Fred, and Helen burn a heap of sticks in the garden lot with their dog Towser helping. Next day they plow the ground with a forked stick to make a garden all their own, and the pie's long story starts from a pumpkin seed.
6450-the-prairie:
James Fenimore Cooper's The Prairie opens with a plea from As You Like It for rest and food in a desert place, then turns to the Louisiana purchase. Much was said and written about adding vast Louisiana to territories already immense and half tenanted, but as controversy cooled, the wisdom of the measure was generally conceded. Nature had barred western extension with desert, yet the purchase gave a belt of fertile country that might have fallen to a rival nation.

It also gave sole command of the great interior thoroughfare and placed countless tribes along the borders within American reach. A mid scene shows a squatter staggering under a fine fat buck while a crouching circle tumbles down dangerous rock passes in impatience, Esther following at measured gait. Cooper writes the prairie as frontier, where settlers, hunters, and native peoples meet on open ground.
64691-eternal-zemmd-must-die:
Henry Hasse wrote the science fiction story Eternal Zemmd Must Die, first printed in Planet Stories in 1949. The blurb tells of something that lanced out of the void at light-speed, stabbed into the Solar System, and vanished. Then corruption began, poison and hate creeping from world to world, before men learned a death blow had been dealt.

The story opens below the Council Room of a peaceful Federation, where DeHarries, Correlator for Earth, crumples his speech and asks what course of action can fight an unseen pattern. Six delegates gather: Aladdian, Empress of Venus, grave and aware of the threat; Kraaj, the huge Jovian emissary, demanding plain speech. Votes from Mars, Mercury, and the outer colonies are still in doubt. DeHarries tells them the Federation faces the greatest crisis it has ever known. Readers get a council-of-worlds mystery about a hidden enemy.
64788-the-secret-dispatch-or-the-adventu:
The Secret Dispatch is a tale of Captain Balgonie by James Grant from Russian past. Its next name counts the deeds of that chief in full. A Chapman house of London brought out this new print of the work. Grant gives the book to Simpson as a mark of high regard. Most turns in it did in truth take place, his front words claim.

He soft the raw wild cast of the tale for his page, he grants. The North Semiramis thirst for rule frames that wild past age. A young rank man wed his kin girl by church leave in the tale frame. Gypsy song in it holds that the Turk moon must fall in time. Part names run from a lost roam man to a fort jail first day.
65368-our-little-tot-s-own-book-of-prett:
Our Little Tot's Own Book, issued in New York by Hurst and Company, bears a copyright of 1912. The full title promises pretty pictures, charming stories, and pleasing rhymes and jingles. Verses about Baby-Land open the book, asking how many miles it lies away.

One flight up and to your right, the verse answers, and please to ring the bell. A prose piece called How Mama Used to Play tells of a happy girlhood on an old green farm. She and her sister owned no store toys, yet played from dawn to dark in places they found. Her pet playhouse was a great stump in the pasture, too wide to reach halfway round. Moss cushions served as chairs, and bits of blue china dressed the dining room shelves.
65669-compete-or-die:
Compete or Die is a science fiction story by Mark Rainsberg, printed in Imagination in February 1957. Its hero, Bart Sponsor, was a Top Competitor who pitied those who were not. One small error made him seek retirement. Yet for him there was only the title's law: compete or die. The story opens at a run.

The narrator slams the aircar door and fumbles for the key. A policeman a hundred feet away wheels at the sound and yells halt. Trembling fingers fail at the ignition. A shot sounds, glass trickles down the narrator's neck, and a hole stands in the windshield level with his eyes. Hands up, the cop calls, close enough now that he can hardly miss. Rainsberg writes a future where competition is the whole of life, and quitting is the one crime.
65786-the-dance-of-dinwiddie:
Marshall Moreton published The Dance of Dinwiddie in nineteen twelve, a long poem in rhymed verse. Dinwiddie is a small town by the Ohio River, near a great bend in the stream. Moreton recalls a dance held at an old country home there.

More than twenty dancers came by high wagon on the night before the dance. Fiddlers played, and a man called the Oracle called the tunes and rhymes. Then flood water rose and closed around the house and barn, leaving them cut off. The poem mixes fond memory, song, and place. Its beat suits the reels and waltzes it recalls.
65887-a-living-lie:
A Living Lie renders Paul Bourget's French novel Mensonges into English. John de Villiers translated it, and Fenno printed it in New York, with Chatto and Windus in London. A long opening letter from Bourget to his translator hopes the book will escape the misconception that greets French novels on Anglo Saxon soil: the reproach of immorality.

Bourget defends the French school that follows Balzac and Stendhal. Balzac called himself a doctor of social sciences, and Stendhal an observer of the human heart. For such writers, analytical precision comes first, and the novelist paints life as it is, ugly truth included. The contents then open on a provincial corner of Paris, with simple souls, a lover and a snob, the dawn of love, and an actress in real life.
65924-hey-ma-where-s-willie:
Hey Ma, Where's Willie?, a short tale by Bukstein, ran in Imagination in October 1952. A farm father tells the story in plain country speech. His son Willie, about fourteen, vanished on a night of strange lights in the hills and odd noises that neighbors called mass illusions.

The father admits he never took to Willie as he did to his five other sons and four daughters. Still, a vanished child nags at him, above all at harvest, when the loss came to light two years past. The family sat at supper after hard work when they found Willie gone. Dry humor and quiet guilt mix in a short, sly take on flying-saucer tales.
66155-no-sons-left-to-die:
Hal Annas imagines a galactic war that eats its young in a tale from Imagination, September 1953. The headnote asks who would replace the boys when there were no sons left to die.

Susan Wildress knows her errand may mean death. She stops eating her ration of ground cedar bark, rabbit, and a hydroponic that tastes like eggplant. She opens a locket inside her sweater. Three years back she watched Darth Brady go out to the ship. He had lied about his age, past seventeen instead of nineteen. The Centers needed boys desperately, so all looked away. A stringent rule barred close ties with boys at the Centers. Even naming the Zeehites near women or children could mean death. Annas builds a grim matriarchy out of one war's hunger.
66188-leave-earthmen-or-die:
A science fiction story by John Massie Davis. Imagination magazine printed it in January 1954. The headnote gives its hook. Three spacemen hear an alien voice warn them off a planet. To each man the voice sounds familiar. One hears a sweetheart, one a son, one a hated enemy. Murph commands the little scout ship.

Radar shows no cities or humanoids below, which cheers him. Then a recorded warning crackles onto every wavelength. Landings here are forbidden under the Interstellar Code, it repeats. Previous colonising attempts have failed, it adds. Forsyth votes to land anyway, and Jamison shrugs agreement. Murph loads combat gear and spirals down regardless. The fleet trails nine hours behind them. Davis builds the tale on that refusal.
66416-three-spacemen-left-to-die:
Russ Winterbotham's Three Spacemen Left To Die comes from Imagination, September 1954. Its blurb states the trap: disease has contaminated the ship, any moment one man may become infected and spray lethal sparks to the others, and there is no cure except prevention.

Commander Al Andrews has sealed the energy-proof bulkheads against the creeping red glow in one quadrant of his circular ship, a revolving wagon-wheel. Only three men remain. Oakey Matthews, young, shaved daily, shoes shined, uniform pressed even in space, watches the instruments. Al, fifty years old and bearded, has lived most of his life out here. He reports Joe in the last stages, then crosses to a drawer and takes out an old-fashioned revolver and a box of shells. The bullets are plastic: strong enough to pierce flesh, too soft to rupture the ship's walls. Oakey begs him not to do it.
66774-let-us-kiss-and-part-or-a-shattere:
Let Us Kiss and Part; or, A Shattered Tie is a dime novel romance by McVeigh Miller. Street and Smith published it in New York as number 943 of the New Eagle Series, under copyrights of 1897 and 1898. Miller wrote many romances of American life for the Eagle series, among them Pretty Madcap Lucy and The Fatal Kiss.

The front matter advertises the publisher's other wares. Street and Smith offer their Diamond Hand Books at ten cents each, clean handbooks by writers who knew their subjects. The titles range from a twentieth century letter writer to a national dream book and a gypsy fortune teller. Boxing, self-defence, hypnotism and army exercises all have their volumes. The novel itself, sold cheap in paper covers, belongs to the great age of the American story paper, when romance reached millions of readers weekly.
66825-forever-we-die:
Forever We Die is a science fiction tale by Thames, printed in Imagination in August 1956. Its hero, Phil Rhodes, sits in a narrow, coffin-shaped cell. A guard spits in his food bowl, shuts the grate, and trudges off down a stone corridor. Darkness returns, and the gruel is tepid in a very cold cell.

Nothing around Rhodes is a whim, the story insists. His broken sleep, the guards' small cruelties, all follow a plan. Rhodes faces the agonies of alien torture because he knows a secret. That secret, the blurb says, holds an entire world in bondage. It proclaims the title's grim law: forever we die. Thames builds the tale as a slow squeeze of dread, with the prisoner's grin as its first act of defiance.
67880-with-perry-on-lake-erie:
James Otis wrote this tale of 1812 with Perry on Lake Erie. Wilde printed it at Boston and Chicago in 1899. William Stecher drew the plates for the boys war story. Otis tells readers no liberty was taken with names or moves.

Much incident came from manuscript sources he held to be sound. All was checked against standard histories of the war, he says. Perry deeds are told from his younger brother view in the tale. The fleet lay useless in Presque Isle bay for lack of men. Otis past war tales with Preble and Porter stand in the same boys series list.
68802-invincible-minnie:
Invincible Minnie is a novel by Holding, put out at New York in the early nineteen twenties. A short word at the front owns the books odd stance at the start. It is not meant to be a tale of love, nor a true to life tale, the author says.

It tells of a thing that did not in fact take place, but of a thing that might well have. If you know a Minnie, as you most like do, the word goes on, you will grant that she could do all the foul deeds told here. She could do a thing, full stop. The parts then roll out her wars in five books, from the first sally to the wreck of men in her path, and a close won in triumph.
69617-pierre-curie:
Marie Curie wrote this life of her husband Pierre Curie, the famed scientist. The book came out in New York in 1923 with Macmillan. Kellogg and co-translator Englished it, with a note on radium facts. A front quote gives Pierre Nobel talk words of 1903.

Pierre warned that radium in criminal hands could prove a great danger. He held that mankind gains more good than evil from new finds. Chapters trace his youth, first science work, and piezo-electric find. Marriage and shared lab life with Marie shape the later pages.
7030-field-and-hedgerow-being-the-last-e:
Richard Jefferies last essays, collected by his widow, fill Field and Hedgerow with country writing. Her preface thanks the Fortnightly Review, Manchester Guardian, Pall Mall Gazette, Standard, and other journals for leave to reprint her husband's latest work. The contents list hours of spring, nature and books, the July grass, winds of heaven, and the country Sunday.

The country side of Sussex, swallow time, Buckhurst Park, house martins among the nuts, and walks in wheat fields follow. Later essays cover just before winter, locality and nature, country places, field words and ways, cottage ideas, and April gossip. Jefferies writes the fields with a naturalist's eye and a poet's patience, to the very end.
70660-why-do-we-die:
T Bodley Scott, a surgeon, wrote this medical book, first published in 1921, subtitled the road to a healthy old age. Press notices quoted on the title page say it argues that premature decay, physical and mental, may within limits be prevented.

Scott opens with a glossary of medical terms, defining ventricle, systole, diastole, atheroma, and the endocrine glands, so lay readers can follow. The contents promise a chapter on the choice of ways, then a long treatment of arterio-sclerosis: its nature, its causes, and the way of safety. A final chapter covers the medicinal treatment of sclerosis. The Lancet commendation calls it wholesome material for thought. Readers of advancing years get a doctor's plain argument against hardening arteries.
709-the-princess-and-curdie:
George MacDonald wrote this sequel to The Princess and the Goblin, in which Curdie, the miner's son, must save the kingdom from a court grown corrupt. Led by a white pigeon and aided by strange beasts, he learns to tell true hands from false ones and to serve a king who has been drugged and misled. The tale moves from mines to palace kitchens and courts.

MacDonald weaves a fable of moral sight: Curdie's gift lets him feel the beast within each person he meets. Lina, the loyal creature at his side, aids him through peril. The book is darker than its predecessor, yet it ends in hope, praising courage, humility, and the hard work of setting a realm right.
7174-the-marquis-of-lossie:
George MacDonald's novel moves from a country stable yard and library through London streets and back again, following a household of sharply drawn folk. Chapter headings name Miss Horn, Kelpie, Lizzy Findlay, Blue Peter, and Florimel, and the action turns on quarrels, a tempest, a portrait, and an old enemy. The Scottish setting stays close even when the scene shifts south.

Lossie gives the book its title and its centre of feeling, while London tests its people against new wealth and new talk. MacDonald lets talk, conscience, and conduct carry the story more than sudden shocks, and the long chapter list promises a tale of manners with a moral pulse. Readers who like broad, humane fiction will find room to settle in.
72662-a-time-to-die:
Harold Calin wrote this science fiction tale for Amazing Stories in June 1961. Finlay illustrated the story of a captain hunting his personal devil in space. Kingsford cleaved the depths in a monomaniacal search, the blurb says at the front, in a cosmic echo of Moby Dick.

Heroes are not brave men, the narrator begins in a cool aside. They are the fortunate victims of circumstance who do not die, he argues. Kingsford returned alone from the first expedition to Aldebaran Nine, and he commands the second, with the narrator as his executive officer, toward the thing that took his crew.
7388-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Old Ironsides is the poem that made Oliver Wendell Holmes famous, and it opens the story told by this volume. Written in 1830, it protested the planned scrapping of the frigate Constitution and helped save the ship. Around it stand the other early poems of 1830 to 1836: The Last Leaf, The Cambridge Churchyard, To an Insect, and The September Gale.

Holmes introduces the collection himself, half apologizing for his trivial verses and letting the better ones shield the worse. That modesty is part of the charm: a young Boston doctor trying out humor, sentiment, and satire in turn. The volume captures a poet at the start, already sure of his wit and his city, not yet the sage of the breakfast table.
74368-the-story-of-wandering-willie:
Story of Wandering Willie is a tale by the author of Effie Friends. Macmillan of London issued the second edition in eighteen seventy. Sir Noel Paton drew the frontispiece for the volume of Highland life. A Scotch song line, Here awa there awa, fronts the tale as motto.

Willie crosses the moors through falling snow as the tale opens. A far village clock struck four, muffled by the storm, some time before. Sunset is past, yet the moor track is not strange to his feet. He trod it when purple heather bloomed, for oh so many years. All the country side knows Wandering Willie and his long lone walks.
74860-elsie:
Elsie, a Christmas story from the Norwegian of Alexander Kjelland, came out at Chicago in 1894. Miles Menander Dawson made the English version and held its copyright from 1889. The tale is set in a house nicknamed Noah's Ark.

Madam Speckbom owns the Ark and lives in its bright rooms on the sunny side. Miss Falbe and her brother lodge above, and a rough crowd called the gang fills the garret nooks. Madam is a wise woman and a quack healer with a sure practice among the poor. The town spreads tales of her cures, and even the better sort repeat them. Her rival is the regular district physician, Bentzen, who jumps at her name. Patients he gives up drift to her door, and she takes a special pride in them.
75031-corrie:
Ruth Lynn tells a child's tale in Corrie, from the Religious Tract Society of London. Lynn had written City Sparrows and The Mysterious Locket. The contents run from Why the Bells Sang and A Walk in the Wood through Father Christmas and the Gardener's Lesson. A tempting bait and a broken vase follow, and Caught, Set Free, and Forest Lodge close the set.

The tale opens on a moonlit street where the bells practice for Christmas morning. Little Corrie lies in her brother Robin's arms, a small ailing sister who has never known how to use her feet. Robin tells her why the bells sing of Jesus and the angels.
75317-when-shadows-die:
Mrs E D E N Southworth wrote When Shadows Die. A L Burt Company issued it at New York. The tale continues her Love's Bitterest Cup. Nearest and Dearest and The Lost Lady of Lone stand hers. A Beautiful Fiend bears her name as well. Meeting and Parting heads chapter one.

The Earl of Enderby travels for his health there. His sister, Mrs Force, travels beside him. His doctor's orders send them both to Germany. Baden-Baden holds their rooms, got by telegram. Mr Force and all his party burst in at breakfast. Three months apart feels like three years there. Leonidas and Odalite pair off at the window. Their present is troubled, their future unsure, it says. It might be for years, it might be forever. Southworth's vast serial world of parted lovers and spa towns kept its hold on readers for decades.
75385-jessie:
Jessie, or Trying to Be Somebody, by Walter Aimwell, is one of the Aimwell Stories, printed at Boston in 1870 by Gould and Lincoln from an 1858 copyright. A preface states the aim of the set: pleasant and instructive lessons for boys and girls. For Jessie, the special object is to kindle a pure and noble ambition in the young, above all in children of misfortune and poverty.

The prize held out is a good name, worth more than rubies, and a conscience void of offence. Chapter heads follow Jessie from a new home and a heavy trunk to work with the Page family. Ronald's flag takes a long, comic stretch: how to make an American flag, the repairs, and the hoisting. Tears, homesickness, and a visit from Henry season the tale of a poor girl placed out to service.
76454-little-king-davie:
Little King Davie is a tale for the young by Nellie Hellis. Its full title adds a verse phrase on kings and priests to God. The book had passed a vast mark of copies by this late print. The book came out in London in the year eighteen ninety seven.

The tale grew from a sermon and a true case in a church mans life. Davie hears a strange call, falls ill, and earns a new name in care. A sore let down and a wish at last won fill the mid parts. Good bye to London and a sweet home close the small warm tale. A print shows the boy at church, ears bent to the word.
76821-the-sureness-of-mackenzie:
Frederick Bechdolt wrote this sea story, calling it an epic of the hill wind and fog. Few jobs hold more thrills than a pilot's, the cover copy argues in its praise. Bringing a big liner into port in fog that hides the decks is that job, it says.

The hill wind and fog raced down from the crest of Tamalpais as the tale opens. Great sirens shook the living rock at the Golden Gate with hoarse warnings there. The Empress came on far out at sea, unswerving, with abiding faith in the man who must conn her home, the pilot whose sureness the title stakes everything on.
77247-lost-nellie:
Lost Nellie and Other Stories, by Pansy, the pen name of Isabella Alden, was published by Lothrop of Boston in 1887. Eight short pieces for children fill the contents: the title tale, An Old Story, Our Jessie, Trying to Amuse Willie, Trouble, Being Good, Lulie's Troubles, and Who'll Settle It. Verse and prose mix in the little volume.

The title piece is a poem. Poor little Nellie, strayed from mamma and papa, is found kneeling under a giant oak, praying to Our Father above. Heaven hears, an angel whispers papa the way, and Nellie is found where she wandered. An Old Story then retells the Flood for small readers. It rained forty days and nights; the good man built a great boat, and those who would not heed him were left outside. The stories that follow keep the same Sunday-school air of warning and comfort.
78627-fifty-fifty-with-bonnie:
Fifty-Fifty with Bonnie is a western story by Tuttle, author of A Bull Movement in Yellow Horse and Fate and a Fool. It opens at the post office of Curlew. Chuck Warner is wailing his favourite song, My Bonnie Lies Over the Ocean, in a minor key, and wiggling his ears in silent accompaniment. The postmaster hands him a letter for Johnny Myers at the Triangle ranch and tells him to deliver it when he feels better.

Chuck is drawn as a full Tuttle grotesque. He has the longest face and the shortest legs west of Bismarck. Hank himself holds a grouch against women, having been jilted, it is rumoured, long ago. The tale is range comedy in Tuttle's tall manner.
79149-the-domestication-of-dobie:
The Domestication of Dobie is a Western tale by Tuttle, author of Making Good for Muley, told as letters from Dobie to his friend Hank. The first letter comes from Mesquite City on June 10. Dobie writes that he is no hand at letters, but he keeps his word, and he and Emmeline are well.

He wants to know who threw a boot at the wedding pair as they boarded the train, since the boot bore a spur that cut his ear. He suspects Windy Wilson and calls him a horse stealing coyote, in strict confidence. Under the jokes sits a tender spot: Dobie wed Emmeline after a few months, and life with her kin is not all smooth.
79222-pie-for-magpie:
Tuttle wrote Pie for Magpie, a comic Western tale told by Ike Harper in rough camp speech. Ike's long time partner is Magpie Simpkins, a tall, gun toting man full of wild plans. A third man, Tellurium Woods, shares their cabin on Plenty Stone Creek. All three hold claims that show work but no pay dirt yet.

Magpie reads of a man who lived thirty days with no clothes and no tools but his bare hands, and he calls the feat a cinch and bets he can match it. Tellurium takes the bet and raises it, and Ike is asked how much cash he can stake. The tale rides on talk, bluff, and pride.
a-monk-of-fife-being-the-chronicle-writt:
Andrew Lang presents his historical novel as the chronicle of Norman Leslie of Pitcullo, now first done into English out of the French, covering the years 1429 to 1431. Norman, a young Scotsman in France, tells how he fled home and joined the fighting around Chinon. The preface links his tale to the real Book of Pluscarden chronicle.

Thirty-two chapters carry Norman through castle escapes, quarrels, and love for a girl named Elliot, into the company of Joan of Arc. He sees the Maid come to Orléans and fights at the bridge and the Augustins. Lang mixes a historian's care for the record with a romancer's love of the Maid's brief, bright career.
aeschylus-lyrical-dramas-blackie:
Aeschylus, the earliest Greek tragedian whose plays survive, wrote in Athens in the fifth century BCE. John Stuart Blackie translated all seven surviving tragedies into English verse. Agamemnon, the Persians, and Prometheus Bound stand among them.

Readers meet the Oresteia trilogy, where murder and justice circle the house of Atreus. Other plays cover Thebes, suppliant women, and the chained Titan Prometheus. Aeschylus is often called the father of tragedy for good reason. Blackie's rendering keeps the grandeur and weight of the Greek. These plays still anchor any serious reading of drama's beginnings.
anna-christie: Eugene O'Neill's play in four acts opens in a New York waterfront saloon and follows Anna Christopherson, daughter of Chris Christopherson, captain of the coal barge Simeon Winthrop. Set about 1910, the action moves from the saloon to the barge at Provincetown and then to Boston, where Anna meets Mat Burke, a stoker from a steamer crew. Family ties, drink and the sea drive the reunions and clashes that follow.
beaumont-and-fletcher-s-works-vol-02-of-:
The Humourous Lieutenant fills this second volume of Beaumont and Fletcher's works, a tragicomedy from the age of Alexander's successors. King Antigonus is billed as an old man with young desires. His son Demetrius loves Celia, who is Enanthe, daughter of King Seleucus. Three kings share Alexander's empire against Antigonus, and the humourous lieutenant, a brave old merry soldier's companion, gives the play its title and its medicine plot.

Celia faces the king's suit with open scorn. Should she be the king's whore, she asks — a brave title — chief commandress of his concubines, hurried from place to place to meet his pleasures? Antigonus calls her a devil for understanding so fast. Leucippe the bawd, physicians, and a love potion that misfires keep the court plot spinning between war and farce.
bonnie-prince-charlie:
G A Henty wrote Bonnie Prince Charlie, a tale of Fontenoy and Culloden, as a boys' historical novel of the Jacobite rising. Henty opens in Glasgow in 1728, where Bailie Anderson takes in a returned prodigal and his small son. That child, Ronald, grows up between Scotland and France.

Ronald serves with the Scots in French service and fights at Fontenoy. News of Prince Charles landing in Scotland draws him home to join the rising of 1745. Marches, coach fights, and narrow escapes fill the middle of the tale. Culloden ends the cause, and Ronald must hide and flee. Henty packs the story with dates, battles, and real names. Young readers learn the last Jacobite war through one loyal young officer's fortunes.
britannica-1911-acadie:
Acadie, or Acadia, was the name the French gave in 1603 to part of the North American mainland between the latitudes of forty and forty-six degrees. The very short Britannica entry exists to fix what the name covered, because later treaties turned on it. When the treaty of Utrecht transferred French possessions to Britain, the words used were Nova Scotia or Acadia.

Readers are sent onward to the Nova Scotia article for the limits included under the term at that date. Even so, the entry makes the key point plain: Acadia was a broad mainland claim, not a single town or harbour, and its loose edges shaped later argument between empires.
britannica-1911-aguado-alexandre-marie:
Aguado, Alexandre Marie, the Spanish banker of 1784 to 1842, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Seville of Jewish parentage, he began as a soldier in Spain's war of independence, fighting for Joseph Bonaparte. After the battle of Baylen in 1808 he joined the French army. There he rose to colonel and aide-de-camp to Marshal Soult.

Exiled in 1815, Aguado set up in Paris as a commission agent, using family links in Havana and Mexico to build wealth fast. Spain gave him full powers to negotiate its loans of 1823, 1828, 1830, and 1831, and rewarded him with a marquis's title and mining grants. He also handled the Greek loan of 1834 and bought the famed wine estate of Chateau Margaux. He died leaving some 60,000,000 francs and a picture collection the French government bought.
britannica-1911-airdrie:
Coal and iron built Airdrie, a burgh of Lanarkshire in Scotland eleven miles east of Glasgow. Its 22,228 people in 1901 could reach that city three ways: by the North British railway, by the Caledonian line through Coatbridge, and by the Monkland Canal, dug between 1761 and 1790. Airdrie had traded as a market town since 1695.

Rich beds of coal and iron close by fed the town's growth. Foundries and machine works gave jobs, and so did woollen and calico mills, silk weaving, paper making, oil, and fireclay. Its public rooms count a town hall, county buildings, a mechanics' institute, a school, two fever hospitals, and a free library. Airdrie was the first town in Scotland to take up the Free Library Act. With Falkirk, Hamilton, Lanark, and Linlithgow it shared one seat in parliament.
britannica-1911-ampere-andre-marie:
André Marie Ampère (1775–1836) was a French physicist born at Polémieux, near Lyons, on 22 January 1775. He delighted in knowledge from infancy. He is said to have worked out long sums with pebbles and biscuit crumbs before he knew figures. His father began teaching him Latin. He stopped on finding the boy's gift for mathematics. Ampère later resumed Latin to master Euler and Bernouilli.

When Lyons fell to the Convention's army in 1793, Ampère's father was executed. He had been a justice of the peace who resisted revolutionary excesses. The shock left the son sunk in apathy for more than a year. Letters on botany revived his interest. He married Julie Carron in 1799. He earned his living giving private lessons at Lyons. The entry closes with his many scientific memoirs and his death at Marseilles on 10 June 1836.
britannica-1911-appert-benjamin-nicolas-:
Benjamin Nicolas Marie Appert (1797-1847) was a French philanthropist who gave his life to prisoners, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells why. He was born in Paris. As a young man he brought a system of mutual teaching into the regimental schools of the Nord, and its success led him to print a manual of the method. While teaching prisoners at Montaigu he fell under suspicion of helping two of them escape.

He was thrown into the prison of La Force. On his release he resolved to spend his life bettering the lot of those whose place he had briefly shared. He travelled widely in Europe studying systems of prison discipline and wrote several books on the subject. After the revolution of 1830 he became secretary to Queen Marie Amélie and organised relief for the needy. He received the Legion of Honour in 1835.
britannica-1911-arnould-plessy-jeanne-sy:
Jeanne Sylvanie Arnould-Plessy was a French stage star who lived from eighteen nineteen to eighteen ninety-seven. She was born at Metz, the child of a town actor. She trained in Paris from age ten and first played at the chief French stage in eighteen thirty-four. Her first role was a huge hit.

She held lead parts for ten years, then left at her peak to wed a play writer in London. Her old house sued her and won a large sum. She played nine years in Russia, then came back to fresh fame. Her last years brought her best work in new plays.
britannica-1911-barbaroux-charles-jean-m:
Charles Jean Marie Barbaroux is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a French leader in revolt from 1767 to 1794. He was schooled at Marseilles and then read law. He rose as a skilled speaker in the courts. He served as clerk to the commune of Marseilles. In 1792 he was sent to Paris on a charge mission. There he joined the Jacobin club and its chiefs.

At his call Marseilles sent troops to Paris that year. Those troops helped in the rising against the king. He was then sent to the Convention by near all votes. From the first he fought the Mountain party hard. He voted for the death of the king with no delay. In the last clash he refused to quit his post. He fled to Caen and then to a town near Bordeaux.
britannica-1911-barnave-antoine-pierre-j:
Antoine Pierre Joseph Marie Barnave (1761–1793) was one of the greatest orators of the first French Revolution, born at Grenoble on 22 October 1761. He came of a Protestant family; his father was an advocate at the Grenoble parlement and his mother a woman of high birth and strong character. Barred as a Protestant from school, he was educated by his mother.

Trained for the law, Barnave made his name at twenty-two with a discourse on the division of political powers. When Dauphiné stirred early toward revolution, his pamphlet on the edicts of May 1788 gave the feeling a voice, and he was elected deputy to the states of Dauphiné. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, follows him to the states-general of 1789 and beyond.
britannica-1911-barrie:
Barrie, the capital of Simcoe county in Ontario, Canada, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica as a town on Lake Simcoe, fifty-six miles north of Toronto. It stood on the Grand Trunk railway and served as a busy centre for the district around it. Its population in 1901 was 5949, making it a modest but active county town of the period.

Local business fills the short entry. Barrie had breweries, carriage factories, boat-building yards, and railway shops, along with works making woollens, stoves, and leather goods. The lake gave it a second role in summer, when visitors came for the resort trade. Barrie was also the starting point for the many steamers that crossed Lake Simcoe, linking the town with other lakeside places during the season.
britannica-1911-bautain-louis-eugene-mar:
Louis Eugène Marie Bautain (1796–1867), a French philosopher and theologian born at Paris, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At the École Normale he fell under the sway of Cousin. He took up higher teaching in 1816 and soon held the chair of philosophy at Strassburg, lecturing there for many years. The swing against free speculation that carried De Maistre and Lamennais touched him too: in 1828 he took holy orders and gave up his university chair.

Faith set above reason is his core claim. Like the schoolmen of old, Bautain kept reason and faith apart: revelation, God's showing of truth, gives facts that reason cannot reach, and philosophy then orders them by method. Yet he held that reason alone can never know things in themselves. A second power, intelligence, links us to unseen truth. At Paris he won fame as a speaker, and taught moral theology from 1853 till his death.
britannica-1911-bervie:
Bervie, also called Inverbervie, is a royal and police burgh in Kincardineshire, Scotland. It sits at the mouth of the Bervie Water. Montrose lies 14 miles south-west, linked by a branch railway. The 1911 Britannica entry gives a 1901 population of 1,207. Its leading trades are woollens, flax, and chemicals. A brisk trade in live-stock is also noted.

David II landed here in 1341, driven in by bad weather with Queen Joanna. In thanks for the town's welcome he granted it a charter, later confirmed by James VI. Hallgreen Castle, a 14th-century stronghold, still stands in repair. South lies Gourdon, a fishing village with boat building and a small harbour trade. At nearby Kinneff the Scottish regalia were hidden during the siege of Dunottar.
britannica-1911-birney-james-gillespie:
James Gillespie Birney (1792–1857) was an American reformer who led the conservative abolitionists from about 1835 to 1845. He was born in Danville, Kentucky, to a wealthy, well-placed family. He graduated at the College of New Jersey, now Princeton, in 1810. He began law practice at Danville in 1814. Politics drew him south to northern Alabama in 1818. There his law career shone, though he himself held slaves for a time.

His father had backed a free-state constitution for Kentucky, and the son's doubts grew. In the Kentucky and Alabama assemblies he fought the return of fugitive slaves across state lines. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his turn to open abolition work in the 1830s. His writings include On the Sin of Holding Slaves and American Churches the Bulwark of American Slavery. He died at Perth Amboy, New Jersey, in November 1857. Two sons served as Federal officers in the Civil War.
britannica-1911-bisceglie:
Bisceglie is a seaport and episcopal see in Apulia, Italy, on the east-south-east coast. It lies in the province of Bari, at a printed distance of 212 miles from Bari by rail. Its population in 1901 was 30,885. The town may match the ancient Natiolum, the 1911 Britannica entry suggests. Two towers still stand from a once strong Norman castle. One of those towers rises some 90 feet high. The cathedral of the town belongs to the same Norman period.

The church of S. Margherita, founded in 1197, is the other building singled out. It holds fine canopied Gothic tombs of the Falcone family. The entry is a short town note of a few lines in total. Castle, cathedral, and the one church carry its whole picture. No trade, history, or port details are given in the text. The Norman past is the town's defining note in this brief record.
britannica-1911-blairgowrie:
Blairgowrie is a small town in Perthshire, Scotland, standing on the river Ericht 16 miles north by east of Perth. It held 3378 people in 1901 and was the end of a branch railway from Coupar Angus. Across a four-arched bridge sits its twin town, Rattray.

The town is modern and grew on water power from the Ericht, which drove linen and jute factories. Sawmills, breweries, and a large works making bee equipment are also listed. Soft fruit, above all strawberries and raspberries, was grown widely round about. The entry adds notes on Loch Clunie to the west, its ruined castle on a crannog, and a mound where a castle once hosted Edward I.
britannica-1911-bougie:
Bougie is a seaport of Algeria, chief town of its arrondissement in the department of Constantine, 120 miles east of Algiers. It climbs the slope of Mount Guraya behind a wall and detached forts built since the French occupation. Behind rise Mounts Babor and Tababort, some 6400 feet high, crowned with fir and cedar forests.

Its old forts, the kasbah built by the Spaniards in 1545, stretches of Roman wall, and Hammadite work of the 1000s give it its interest. The streets are so steep that many are climbed by stairs. The harbour, enlarged from 1897 to 1902, covers 63 acres with 23 to 30 feet of water. As the natural port of Kabylia its trade in oils, wools, hides, and minerals grew greatly under French rule. The town held 10,419 people in 1906.
britannica-1911-boulanger-george-ernest-:
George Ernest Jean Marie Boulanger (1837–1891) was a French general. His ride to fame as war minister shook the republic. Born at Rennes, he entered the army in 1856. He served in Algeria, Italy, Cochin-China, and the Franco-German War. He earned a name as a smart soldier. He became a brigadier-general in 1880, on the duc d'Aumale's word.

As war minister in 1886 he struck that same duke's name from the army list. The strike was part of the campaign against the princes. The debt was remembered against him. As director of infantry from 1882 he had made himself known as a reformer. In Tunis in 1884 he clashed with the political resident and was recalled. He held office under Freycinet, with Clemenceau's backing. The entry follows his reforms, his popular cult, his fall, and his flight and death in 1891.
britannica-1911-brie:
Brie is a farming district of northern France east of Paris, bounded west and south by the Seine and north by the Marne. Its 2400 square miles cover most of Seine-et-Marne plus parts of five other departments. The west was called Brie francaise and the east Brie champenoise, a split the entry keeps in view.

The land is a plateau with few rises. It stands 300 to 500 feet high in the west and 500 to 650 feet in the east. Large woods such as Senart, Crecy and Armainvilliers break its surface. Clay topsoil holds bits of siliceous sandstone used for millstones and building, over a limestone base. Rain is light, only 20 to 24 inches, and rivers are few, chiefly the Yeres and the Grand and Petit Morin. Grain and dairy goods, above all its cheeses, made the district famed.
britannica-1911-brochant-de-villiers-and:
Andre Jean Francois Marie Brochant de Villiers (1772–1840) was a French mineralogist and geologist born at Villiers, near Nantes, on 6 August 1772. After the Ecole Polytechnique he was, in 1794, the first pupil admitted to the Ecole des Mines. In 1804 he became professor of geology and mineralogy there while the school sat at Pezay in Savoy.

He returned with the school to Paris in 1815 and later rose to inspector general of mines and member of the Academy of Sciences. His field studies covered the transition strata of the Tarantaise, the place of granite rocks at Mont Blanc, and the lead minerals of Derbyshire and Cumberland. He also oversaw the making of the geological map of France, carried out by his pupils Dufrenoy and Elie de Beaumont. His books include an elementary treatise on mineralogy (1801-1802) and a shortened treatise on crystallography (1818). He died in Paris on 16 May 1840.
britannica-1911-buckie:
Buckie is a fishing town in Banffshire, Scotland. It stands on the Moray Firth, at the mouth of Buckie burn. It lies about 17 miles west of Banff. This 1911 Britannica entry gives its harbour and trades. The town is a police burgh with a railway station. Its population was 5849 in 1891. By 1901 it had risen to 6549.

Buckie draws one of the largest Scottish herring fleets. The fleet gathers there in the herring season. The town is also the chief seat of line fishing in Scotland. Its harbour has an outer and an inner basin. The basins cover 9 acres in all. Quayage runs to half a mile. Other trades include engineering works and distilleries. Rope, sail and oil works also employ local people. The entry notes Portgordon, a fishing village to the west. It also notes Danish cairns near Rathven, to the east.
britannica-1911-carnoustie:
Carnoustie is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a police burgh and watering-place in Forfarshire, Scotland, with a population of 5204 in 1901. The town lies on the North Sea, about ten and three-quarter miles east-north-east of Dundee on the North British railway. Bathing and golfing draw its visitors. South of the town, Barry Links forms a triangular sandy tract at the shire's south-eastern corner.

The entry notes that Barry Links serves as a camping and training ground for artillery and infantry. Its far point, Buddon Ness, stands off dangerous shoals called the Roaring Lion, named for the deep boom of the waves there. Two lighthouses rise on the Ness at different heights, their lights visible from 13 and 16 miles away. The result is a short portrait of a small coastal town shaped by the sea and by the army.
britannica-1911-caro-elme-marie:
Elme Marie Caro (1826–1887) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French philosopher born at Poitiers, where his father taught philosophy. He studied at the Stanislas College and the École Normale, graduating in 1848, then taught at several provincial universities. He came to Paris in 1858 and took the philosophy chair at the Faculty of Letters in 1864. The French Academy received him in 1874.

Caro spent his career defending Christianity against modern Positivism, and the philosophy of Cousin shaped his thought. The entry judges his strength to lie in exposition and criticism rather than in fresh ideas. His books cover mysticism in the eighteenth century, the idea of God, materialism and science, and pessimism in his own century. He also wrote studies of Littré and of George Sand, and he contributed widely to French journals before his death in Paris.
britannica-1911-champmesle-marie:
Marie Champmesle, a French stage player of high fame, gets a life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Rouen in sixteen forty two, she came of a good house there. Her birth name was Desmares, from her father side. She first trod the stage at Rouen with the man she wed in sixteen sixty six. By sixteen sixty nine the pair played in Paris halls.

Her turn as Hermione in a Racine play won her great fame in one year. Racine wrote some of his best sad plays for her voice and art. Weak plays oft lived by her true style and sad force alone. Phedre stood as the peak of her stage wins in the text. She helped open the Comedie Francaise in sixteen eighty and held its top sad roles for years.
britannica-1911-collins-william-wilkie:
William Wilkie Collins (1824–1889) was an English novelist, elder son of the landscape painter William Collins. He was born in London on 8 January 1824. He was schooled in private at Highbury. At age twelve he went with his parents to Italy for three years. That stay shaped his first novel in time.

Back in England he was set to the tea trade, then left it for law. He entered Lincoln's Inn in 1846 and was called to the bar in 1849. Law pleased him little, though its lore served his plots later. On his father's death he turned to letters. His life of his father came out in 1848. Antonina, his first fiction, followed in 1850. Basil and Hide and Seek came next. Friendship with Dickens grew in those years. The entry praises his grip on readers and the craft of his plots. Count Fosco stands as his master stroke.
britannica-1911-collot-d-herbois-jean-ma:
Jean Marie Collot d'Herbois (1750–1796) was a French revolutionary born in Paris and an actor by trade. He worked for years at the chief provincial theatres of France and Holland. He then directed the playhouse at Geneva. He had a share in the unrest from the first. Real weight came to him only in 1791.

A small book made his name that year. L'Almanach du Père Gérard set out the gains of a constitutional monarchy in homely style. It won him great fame at a stroke. He then spoke up for Swiss soldiers sent to the galleys for mutiny at Nancy. His work freed them. His views grew more radical with time. He sat in the Commune of Paris in August 1792. In September he joined the Committee of Public Safety. The Convention sent him to Lyons in October 1793 to punish the city.
britannica-1911-coolgardie:
Coolgardie is a municipal town in Western Australia, 310 miles by rail east of Perth. It stands 528 miles by rail north-east of Albany. Its people numbered 4,249 in 1901. Gold-fields found in 1891 rank among the richest in the colony. That find made the town and still feeds it.

Other minerals lie in the ground as well. Lignite, copper, graphite and silver all occur there. Toorak and Montana form small home suburbs of the town. One great work of engineering closes the entry. A full water supply was brought to the town from Fremantle, more than 330 miles in a straight line. That scheme was finished in 1903. The entry is short, and those facts form its whole stock.
britannica-1911-findlay-john-ritchie:
John Ritchie Findlay (1824-1898) was a Scottish newspaper owner and philanthropist, and his career is told in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Arbroath and educated at Edinburgh University, he joined the Scotsman, first in its publishing office, then on its editorial side. He became a partner in 1868 and inherited most of the property in 1870.

The entry credits his energy for much of the paper's growth in reach and sales, which brought him a fortune he spent on public gifts. He gave the nation the Scottish National Portrait Gallery, opened in Edinburgh in 1889 at a cost of over 70,000 pounds. He refused a baronetcy and held the freedom of Edinburgh from 1896.
britannica-1911-fontan-louis-marie:
Louis Marie Fontan (1801-1839), French man of letters, was born at Lorient on 4 November 1801. He began as a clerk in a government office and was dismissed for taking part in a political banquet. At nineteen he went to Paris and wrote for the Tablettes and the Album. Brought to trial for political articles in the Album, he defended himself so fiercely that his case was put off without end. The paper was suppressed for a time, while Fontan published political poems and plays.

His play Perkins Warbec of 1828, written with Halevy and Drouineau, was the most successful of his stage works. When the Album revived, Fontan printed in it a sharp, witty attack on Charles X, in June 1829. To escape prosecution he fled across the frontier. Finding no safe shelter abroad, he returned to France, as the entry follows his short, combative career.
britannica-1911-gay-marie-francoise-soph:
Marie Francoise Sophie Gay (1776-1852) was a French author, born in Paris on 1 July 1776. The 1911 Britannica entry gives her two marriages: first to a broker, Liottier, ending in divorce in 1799, then to M. Gay, a revenue official. His post brought her into the company of the day's leading writers, musicians, actors and painters, and her salon drew them all.

Her writing began with a letter of 1802 defending Madame de Stael's Delphine, and a first novel, Laure d'Estell, the same year. Sainte-Beuve judged Leonie de Montbreuse of 1813 her best work, though Anatole, the tale of a deaf-mute, may be better known. The entry also names her Salons celebres, her comedies and opera libretti, and songs with her own words and music. She died in Paris on 5 March 1852.
britannica-1911-gillie:
Gillie is a Scots word explained in a short note in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It comes from Gaelic words for a servant or boy. At first it named a man who served a Gaelic chief, a use now rare save in tales of the past.

In the Highlands of Scotland the word now names the man who goes with a sportsman to shoot or fish. A gillie-wetfoot, a term now out of use, was the man whose task was to carry his master across streams. Lowland folk used the word in scorn for the train of men who followed a Highland chief.
britannica-1911-gowrie: Gowrie is a belt of rich low land in Perthshire in Scotland, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It runs along the north shore of the Firth of Tay, from Perth toward Dundee. It is fifteen miles long and two to four miles wide. Once boggy, it has been drained and farmed, and is now one of the most fertile tracts in Perthshire. Many castles and great houses dot the district.
britannica-1911-halevy-jacques-francois-:
Jacques François Fromental Élie Halévy (1799–1862) was a French composer. He was born in Paris on 27 May 1799. He came from a Jewish family. At the Paris Conservatoire he studied under Berton and Cherubini. In 1819 he won the grand prix de Rome. His prize cantata was Herminie. Rome gave him years of study in Italian music. His first Paris opera, L'Artisan, came in 1827.

Two works of 1835 founded his fame. La Juive was his great tragic opera. L'Éclair was a comic opera of curious design. It uses two tenors and two sopranos, with no chorus. Eléazar's air in La Juive became famous across France. Halévy taught at the Conservatoire from 1827 until death. Gounod, Massé and Bizet were among his pupils. He died at Nice on 17 March 1862.
britannica-1911-jacquard-joseph-marie:
Joseph Marie Jacquard, a French inventor who lived from 1752 to 1834, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Lyons, son of a working weaver. On his father's death he inherited two looms and set up on his own. When trade failed him, he burned lime at Bresse while his wife plaited straw.

Jacquard fought in the defence of Lyons in 1793 and later served as a soldier. His young son was shot down at his side. Back at Lyons, he worked in a factory and spent spare hours on an improved loom. He showed the loom at Paris in 1801 and was placed at a national school of arts. A loom by Vaucanson there suggested changes that perfected his own. Silk weavers fought the machine fiercely, fearing for their living. Still, by 1812 eleven thousand Jacquard looms were at work in France.
britannica-1911-kingussie:
Kingussie is a town in Inverness shire, Scotland, and a short gazetteer entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica notes its site and hopes. The town held 987 people in 1901. It stands 750 feet above the sea, on the left bank of the Spey. A bridge crosses the river at the town, and the Highland railway serves it.

The duke of Gordon founded Kingussie toward the end of the eighteenth century. He hoped it would become a centre of woollen manufacture. That hope was not met in the event. In time the place grew popular as a health resort instead. The scenery in every direction is praised as fine. Across the river lies Ruthven, where James Macpherson was born in 1736.
britannica-1911-kovalevsky-sophie:
Sophie Kovalevsky (1850–1891) was a Russian mathematician, born at Moscow on the 15th of January 1850, the daughter of General Corvin-Krukovsky. Like many young Russian women of her time, she longed for study, but her own country's universities were closed to women. In 1868 she made a formal marriage with a young student, Waldemar Kovalevsky, and the two went to Germany. She studied at Heidelberg, then read in private with Karl Weierstrass at Berlin from 1871 to 1874.

In 1874 Göttingen gave her a degree in absentia on the strength of three dissertations, on subjects that included Saturn's rings. After her husband's death in 1883 she took a post at Stockholm, and in 1884 she became a full professor there. In 1888 she won the Prix Bordin of the Paris Academy for work on the motion of a solid body round a fixed point. She died at Stockholm on the 10th of February 1891.
britannica-1911-kyrie:
The Kyrie, in full kyrie eleison, is a Greek phrase meaning "Lord, have mercy." The words are a prayer used at the start of the Mass and in other offices of the Eastern and Roman Churches. In the Anglican Book of Common Prayer the Kyrie stands in the orders for Morning and Evening Prayer. It also comes, with an added petition, as the people's response after each of the Ten Commandments at the opening of the Communion Service.

Since these responses are usually sung, the name Kyrie is also given to their musical setting. In the Lutheran Church the Kyrie is still said or sung in the first Greek. A shortened form of the words, "Kyrielle," names a kind of verse: four lines of eight syllables, with the last line repeated in each verse as a refrain.
britannica-1911-legendre-adrien-marie:
Adrien Marie Legendre, a French mathematician who lived from 1752 to 1833, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Paris in 1752, though some accounts say Toulouse. He was brought up at Paris. He finished his studies at the Collège Mazarin.

His first published writings formed part of a treatise on mechanics from 1774. That work was by the Abbé Marie, his professor. Legendre's name, though, is not mentioned in it. Soon after, he was made professor of mathematics at the École Militaire in Paris. He later held a chair at the École Normale. In 1782 the Berlin Academy gave him its prize. The prize was for a memoir on the paths of projectiles in resisting media. The article follows a scholar whose name now marks deep results in his science.
britannica-1911-mealie: Mealie is the South African name for Indian corn or maize, and this very short 1911 Britannica entry explains where the word came from. The spelling follows the Cape Dutch sound of milje. That Dutch form was itself taken from the Portuguese milho, with the added sense of the millet of India. In South Africa the name was used for maize.
britannica-1911-menomonie:
Menomonie is a city in Wisconsin and the seat of Dunn county, on the Red Cedar river. The 1911 Britannica article puts it about sixty-four miles east of Saint Paul, Minnesota. Its count in 1910 was 5,036, down from 5,655 in 1900. Two rail lines serve the town. It was settled about 1846 and gained a city charter in 1882. Its grain lifts and mills mark it as a farm market town.

The city is best known for schools and halls set up by James Huff Stout, a rich local lumberman. Among them are a memorial library, a county farm school, and the Stout Institute. That school trains teachers of home science and gives town children training of the body. In 1896 Stout set up there the first free travelling library in the state. Town works make bricks, tiles, carriages, and flour, and trade in dairy goods and stock.
britannica-1911-milngavie: Milngavie, a police burgh of Dumbartonshire in Scotland, is described in this short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Its name is locally pronounced Millguy. The town held 3,481 people in 1901 and lies six miles north-west of Glasgow by rail. Its chief industries include bleach-fields, dye-works, a distillery, and a paper mill. Yet the town is largely a home suburb for Glasgow business men. Two reservoirs near it, Mugdock and Craigmaddie, store water from Loch Katrine. Mugdock Castle, an old Graham stronghold, stands nearby.
britannica-1911-moreau-de-saint-mery-med:
Médéric Louis Élie Moreau de Saint Méry (1750–1819) was a French politician born at Fort de France, Martinique, on the 28th of January 1750. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows him to Paris at nineteen, to the bar, and back to Martinique to practise law. In 1780 he joined the colonial council of San Domingo.

Sent to study the laws of the French colonies, he published their laws and constitutions from 1550 to 1785. In 1789 he headed the assembly of the electors of Paris and sat for Martinique in the Constituent Assembly. His moderate views brought his arrest after the 10th of August 1792, but he escaped to America. There he kept a bookshop in Philadelphia and wrote a great survey of Saint-Domingue. Back in France he helped draft the colonial code and governed Parma, Piacenza, and Guastalla until 1806.
britannica-1911-osawatomie:
Osawatomie, a city in Miami county in Kansas, is described in a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands about forty five miles south of Kansas City on a rail line. Close to five thousand people lived there at the later count in the entry. A state hospital for the insane stands a mile away.

Farming land around the town is good, and gas and oil are found nearby. The town was settled about 1854 by colonists sent by the Emigrant Aid Company. Its name joins parts of the words Osage and Pottawatomie. In the Border War it saw two attacks by pro slavery men from Missouri. In August 1856 John Brown and about forty men tried to hold it and were beaten. The town was looted and near destroyed. A park marks the battle.
britannica-1911-pardessus-jean-marie:
Jean Marie Pardessus, a French lawyer who lived from 1772 to 1853, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Blois, he was taught by the Oratorians and then read law, first under his own father, a pupil of Pothier. Widowed at twenty seven, he refused to wed again and give his children a stepmother.

His treatise on servitudes of 1806 ran through eight editions, and a work on bills of exchange marked him out for a new chair in trade law at Paris. He won that chair in open contest in 1810, and his lectures came out as a course in four volumes. Voters sent him to the chamber in 1815 and kept him there till 1830. He then refused the oath to Louis Philippe and lost his post. His great set of old sea laws, gathered from before the seventeen hundreds, rounds out the account.
britannica-1911-pie:
Pie is a word article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica that sorts out the senses of a short English word. The first sense is the bird more often called the magpie. The word comes through French from the Latin pica. From the bird's black and white look, the name passed to other mixed things.

One such thing was the ordinal, a church table that showed how movable feasts changed the fixed services. An English act of 1549 banned pies along with other old service books. The bird's patchy look also gives us piebald, for a horse marked with large black and white patches. Where the second colour is not black, the right word is skewbald. A second main sense is the dish: meat, fish, or fruit baked in a crust of pastry.
britannica-1911-prairie:
Prairie, a word taken from the French for a meadow tract, is defined in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as flat grass land with no trees. In strict use the word is held to such tracts in the central parts of North America. The entry then draws the bounds of that vast grass sea.

In the United States the grass runs from south Michigan and west Ohio across a chain of states. Illinois is marked as the Prairie State in its own right. The grass runs west of the great river to the foot hills of the Rocky range. In Canada it runs from those same hills to a line east of Winnipeg. The word feeds a host of joined names for birds, beasts, and plants of the grass. One such name is the prairie hen, a grouse of the plains.
britannica-1911-ramie:
Ramie is a fibre article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Ramie, also called rhea or China-grass, comes from plants of the genus Boehmeria. That genus belongs to the nettle order and is close kin to the stinging nettle. It differs from the nettle in one welcome way: it has no stinging hairs.

The entry first clears up a tangle of names. Two plants hide behind the three terms in trade. One is Boehmeria nivea, the China-grass of commerce. Chinese growers have raised it from very early times under their own name for it. The other, perhaps a variety of the same species, is the true ramie. It comes from the Malay Islands, where its name is Malay, and from Assam as rhea. The article sorts the names before turning to the shrubby plant itself. Growers and spinners who met these fibres in trade will find their identities fixed here.
britannica-1911-sault-sainte-marie:
Sault Sainte Marie, a city in Michigan, is surveyed in a long place entry in the 1911 Britannica. It is the county seat of Chippewa county, on Saint Mary's river at the outlet of Lake Superior. Its count rose from 5,760 in 1890 to 12,615 in 1910, half of them foreign born in 1900. Three railways serve it, and a bridge ties it to the Canadian town of the same name.

The river falls 20 feet in less than a mile, and lock canals make it passable for deep ships. The works run from a fur company lock of 1797 to the great Poe lock of 1896. In 1907 more freight passed here than any other canal in the world, over 58 million tons. The place was long a Chippewa fishing ground, first reached by French missionaries in 1641.
britannica-1911-stefanie:
Stefanie is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a lake in East Africa. The lake is also called Basso Naebor or Chuwaha. It lies far south in a chain of lakes in the great rift zone. At about forty miles long and fifteen miles wide, it is the lowest lake in that chain. Its height above the sea is given as 1880 feet.

The lake has no outlet, so its size shifts with rain and flow. Its main feeder is the Dulei, which flows in at the north end. That stream is joined by the Galana Sagan on its way south. At low water the west part of the lake runs dry. Hills east of the lake form a marked watershed.
britannica-1911-stephen-sir-leslie:
Sir Leslie Stephen, an English writer and critic who lived from 1832 to 1904, is the subject of a long life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came from a famed family of lawyers and officials. His grandfather knew Wilberforce, and his father served for years as a colonial under-secretary. Leslie was born at Kensington Gore in London in 1832.

He studied at Eton, at King's College in London, and at Trinity Hall in Cambridge. He stayed on there as a fellow and tutor. At home he had met the Clapham group and men of letters from his youth. He wrote sketches of Cambridge life for the papers. He married first a daughter of Thackeray, and later Julia Prinsep. In time he gave up holy orders, which he had taken as a young fellow.
britannica-1911-tait-peter-guthrie:
Peter Guthrie Tait (1831-1901) was a Scottish physicist, born at Dalkeith, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. After schooling at Edinburgh he went to Peterhouse, Cambridge, and graduated in 1852 as senior wrangler and first Smith's prizeman. He stayed two years as a fellow, then took the chair of mathematics at Queen's College, Belfast.

At Belfast he worked with Thomas Andrews on the density of ozone and other gases, and was led by him to Hamilton and to quaternions. In 1860 Tait took the chair of natural philosophy at Edinburgh, holding it almost until his death. He became the leading voice on quaternions after Hamilton, writing two textbooks on them. From 1864 he also did original work in heat science and other branches of physics, both in theory and by test.
britannica-1911-tempest-marie:
Marie Tempest, the stage name of an English actress born in 1866, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Her birth name was Marie Susan Etherington. In 1898 she married an actor and playwright who was a grandson of the fifth duke of Richmond. She had a charming soprano voice and was trained for opera and concert work.

Yet she first appeared in light comic opera, where she became very popular, the entry says. Leaving music for the comedy stage, she won an even greater success as an actress. Her Becky Sharp of 1901 is singled out. In later years, under her own management, she staged a run of modern comedies in London. Her skill there matched the triumphs of a famed Paris actress.
britannica-1911-tussaud-marie:
Marie Tussaud (1760-1850), founder of the famed London show of wax figures, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Berne, she was the daughter of an army officer who died the year she was born. Her uncle, a doctor there, had won note for his fine wax models of the body. He gave up medicine for wax work as a fine art and moved to Paris.

The article says his house drew many gifted men of the day. He brought his niece there at six and taught her to model in wax. She grew so skilled that she modelled many great people of France while still young. She was even called to the palace to teach the king's sister the craft. From her uncle's show the mob took the wax busts it carried in the first bloody march of the Revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-corbi:
Ambrose Corbie, also Corby or Corbington, was born near Durham on 7 December 1604 and died at Rome on 11 April 1649. Fourth son of Gerald Corbie and Isabella Richardson, exiles for the Faith, he entered St-Omer's at twelve and the English College at Rome in 1622. He entered the Jesuits at Watten in 1627, professed in 1641. After teaching at St-Omer's and serving as Ghent minister in 1645, he became confessor at Rome's English College, dying in his forty-fifth year.

His Certamen Triplex tells the martyrdom of three English Jesuits: Thomas Holland, his brother Ralph Corbie, and Henry Morse. It was published at Antwerp in 1645 with three engraved portraits. His parents, by agreement, also entered religion: his father as a Jesuit lay brother in 1628, his mother professed Benedictine at Ghent in 1633, dying a centenarian in 1652.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ange-de-saint:
His real name was Francois Vaffard. Ange de Sainte Rosalie, a French genealogist and friar of the Petits-Peres of the Discalced Augustinians, was born at Blois in 1655 and died in Paris in 1726. After his religious profession in 1672, he held many important offices in his order's houses. In the end he gave himself to genealogy, contributing extensively to Moreri's Grande dictionnaire historique.

From materials collected by Pere Anselme and Caille de Fourny, he prepared a genealogical and chronological history of the royal house of France and its great officers of the crown. Death left it unfinished, but his collaborator Pere Simplicien completed it. Three further volumes also came from Simplicien. Among his other works is L'Etat de la France, which the Benedictines of Saint-Maur edited in 1749. A supplementary volume covers the coronation, the armorial bearings, and the prerogatives of France's kings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-d-abb:
Antoine d'Abbadie, a French astronomer and explorer born in 1810, spent ten years mapping Ethiopia after six years of study. With his younger brother Arnauld beside him, he surveyed highland positions, collected manuscripts, and pressed for Catholic missions in the region. His science served both geography and faith.

Back in France, Antoine gave his Abbadia estate to the Paris Academy of Sciences, funding research and an observatory meant to catalogue half a million stars. His books list Ethiopian manuscripts and record his triangulations, while Arnauld's memoir recalls twelve years in the highlands. The entry honours two brothers who joined field science to missionary zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-masso:
Antoine Massoulie, a French Dominican theologian born at Toulouse in 1632, prized study above office. He turned down a bishopric and sought release from duties that distracted him, so he could teach and write. He knew the Summa of Saint Thomas by heart and spoke Greek and Hebrew fluently, debating rabbis in public at Avignon and Florence.

His books defended the Thomist doctrine of physical premotion, God's action on free agents, against rival views. Others attacked the Quietists, a movement he opposed by setting out true prayer in Thomist terms. His chief works appeared at Rome, Toulouse, and Paris, and the entry presents a scholar whose learning served debate and devotion alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-armand-de-la-:
Armand de la Richardie, born at Périgueux on 7 June 1686 and dead at Quebec on 17 March 1758, entered the Society of Jesus at Bordeaux in 1703. He was sent to the Canada mission in 1725. He spent two years helping Father Pierre Daniel Richer in Lorette and learning the Huron language. In 1728 the priest went to Detroit to restore the long-broken mission among the dispersed Petun-Hurons in the West, finding not one professing Christian, though many aged people had been baptized.

The new Indian church, seventy cubits long, could barely hold the fervent congregation of practising Hurons. On the night of 24 to 25 March 1746 he was struck by paralysis, and on 29 July he was carried in an open canoe to Quebec. In 1747 the Hurons insisted he return to restore peace to their nation, and, almost recovered, he set out from Montreal on 10 September and reached Detroit on 20 October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auguste-theod:
Auguste Theodore Paul de Broglie was an abbe, professor of apologetics at the Catholic Institute of Paris, born at Auteuil in 1834, who died in 1895. He was the son of the Duc de Broglie and Albertine de Stael, a Protestant daughter of Madame de Stael. His mother died young, and his Protestant aunt raised him, working to make a Christian of him in a church not her own. He entered the navy, rose to lieutenant, and felt a call to the priesthood.

Ordained in 1870, he spent his life as a defender of Catholic dogma. His chief work was his History of Religions. His pieces covered positivism, Zoroastrian and Vedic faith, Buddhism, Islam, Israel, and the idea of God in the Testaments. At his death, caused by an insane person's violence, he was at work on a book joining reason and faith. Two posthumous works were edited by Abbe Piat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-athanas:
Athanase Charles Marie Charette de la Contrie was born at Nantes in 1832 and died at Basse-Motte in 1911. His father was nephew to General Charette, shot at Nantes in 1795 during the Vendée rising. His birth was concealed, since his mother hid with the Duchesse de Berry and his father was sought by police. Unwilling as a legitimist to serve Louis Philippe, he entered Turin's Military Academy in 1846 and left in 1848.

After Austrian service under Modena's duke, he went to Rome in 1860 and served Pius IX, captaining the first Franco-Belgian Volunteers. Wounded at Castelfidardo that September, he later led the Pontifical Zouaves and was made a French general. Elected to the National Assembly, he resigned without sitting, choosing to remain at the pope's disposal. His Zouaves mustered out in 1871, and his last thirty years served religion and hopes of monarchy's restoration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-defender-of-t:
A canon law entry describes the Defender of the Matrimonial Tie, the official who defends the marriage bond in cases over a marriage's validity or nullity. Benedict XIV introduced the office by his Bull Dei Miseratione in 1741, to guard against abuses in ordinary procedure. Annulments had followed when only one spouse sought freedom, while the other connived, lacked funds, or could not appeal.

Scandal grew from frequent dissolutions with freedom to remarry. The Bull requires each diocese's ordinary to appoint a defender, upright and learned in law, a cleric if possible, a layman if necessary. He must be cited to every trial on validity, or proceedings are null. He examines witnesses and argues, orally or in writing, whatever favours the marriage's validity, and may appeal against an adverse sentence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eliza-maria-g:
Eliza Maria Gillespie, in religion Mother Mary of Saint Angela, founded Holy Cross women's work in America. She was born in Pennsylvania in 1824 and died at Notre Dame, Indiana, in 1887.
