Daughter of John Purcell Gillespie, she studied with the Dominican sisters at Somerset and at the Visitation Convent in Georgetown, finishing in 1844. With her cousin Eleanor Ewing she raised a large sum for famine-stricken Ireland.

Feeling a call in 1853, she went to Notre Dame to farewell her brother. There she met Father Edward Sorin. She joined the struggling Holy Cross community instead of the Sisters of Mercy. She took the habit that year, trained at Caen in France, and professed in December 1853. Back in America she led Saint Mary's Academy at Bertrand, moved it near Notre Dame in 1855, and won it a state charter. In the Civil War she organised Holy Cross sisters to nurse the wounded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-erie:
The Diocese of Erie was established in 1853 and embraces thirteen counties of northwestern Pennsylvania, an area of 10,027 square miles. It was under the French flag and the See of Quebec from 1753 to 1758. It was under the English flag and the Vicariate Apostolic of London from 1758 to the Treaty of Paris in 1783.

In August 1843 the Diocese of Pittsburg was formed. It included all of Pennsylvania west of a line along the eastern border of six counties: Bedford, Huntingdon, Clearfield, Elk, McKean, and Potter. That land is the territory of the present Diocese of Erie. In 1853 Michael O'Connor, the first Bishop of Pittsburg, petitioned the Holy See for a division of his diocese, and took for himself the poorest part, becoming the first Bishop of Erie. When he assumed government on 29 July 1853, there were only twenty-eight churches, eleven secular priests, and three Benedictine Fathers for Catholics scattered through the thirteen counties.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guy-lefevre-d:
Norman Orientalist Guy Lefèvre de la Boderie, born near Falaise in 1541, learned Hebrew and Syriac so he could draw nearer, through Christ's own tongue, to the mind of Christ. Studying under Guillaume Postel at the Collège de France, he published the Syriac New Testament in a Latin rendering in 1560. He was called to Antwerp in 1568 to help build the great Polyglot Bible.

His collated Syriac New Testament with Latin version appeared in the Polyglot's fifth volume in 1572, beside a Syriac grammar, a dictionary, and a primer for beginners. Back in France as secretary to the Duke of Alençon, he kept his Catholic faith among radical friends and wrote apologetic poems like La Galliade. He died in his birth house in 1598, leaving an epitaph that prized seeking truth over amassing treasure.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-victo:
French statesman and historian Jacques Victor Albert, duc de Broglie, was born at Paris on 13 June 1821. He died there on 19 January 1901. After a brief diplomatic career he resigned to devote himself to letters. His work L'Église et l'Empire romain au IVe siècle, six volumes from 1856, won him Lacordaire's seat in the French Academy in 1862. In 1871 he became ambassador to England.

He was recalled in 1872 and took his Assembly seat. He soon led opposition to the Republic and to Thiers. Twice president of the council, in 1873 and 1877, he was finally defeated in his own district. He then withdrew from public life. Besides editing his father's souvenirs and Talleyrand's memoirs, he published works on Louis XV's diplomacy. Those placed him in the first rank of historians. The entry presents a scholar-statesman of monarchist France.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-tyrie:
Theologian James Tyrie was born at Drumkilbo, Perthshire, Scotland, in 1543. He died at Rome on 27 May 1597. Educated first at St Andrews, he joined Edmund Hay during de Gouda's mission. In Hay's company he went to Rome and entered the Society of Jesus. He was sent to Clermont College, Paris, in June 1567, where Hay had become rector. He remained there in various posts until 1590.

He served as professor and, from 1585, head of the Scottish Jesuit mission. During that period he disputed with Knox, answering him in The Refutation of ane Answer, published at Paris in 1573. Next year he privately discussed religion with Andrew Melville in Paris. In 1585 he was summoned to Rome as France's representative on the Committee of Six. That committee drew up Acquaviva's first Ratio Studiorum, printed in 1586. The entry presents a Scottish Jesuit of controversy and curriculum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-leslie:
John Leslie was the Scottish Bishop of Ross who never wavered in loyalty to Mary Queen of Scots. Born in 1527 of the House of Leslie of Balquhain, apparently illegitimate, he studied at Aberdeen and in France. He graduated doctor of laws, became professor of canon law at Aberdeen, and was ordained in 1558. In 1561 he went to France to bring the young queen home.

Made privy councillor in 1565 and Bishop of Ross the same year, he also served as judge and co-editor of Scotland's laws. After Mary's escape from Lochleven in 1568 he joined her and acted as her chief commissioner at York. He was imprisoned at Ely and in the Tower for favoring her marriage to the Duke of Norfolk. Banished after his release in 1573, he pleaded her cause at European courts and Rome, dying near Brussels in 1596, restored in dignity but never returning home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lavigerie:
Charles Martial Lavigerie (1825-1892) was a French cardinal, born near Bayonne, trained at Larressore, St. Nicolas-du-Chardonnet, and St. Sulpice, and ordained in June 1849. A year of higher study at the Ecole des Carmes brought Sorbonne doctorates in letters in 1850 and theology in 1853, later joined by Roman law doctorates.

Chaplain of Sainte-Genevieve and Sorbonne church history professor from 1854, he organized Catholic student circles and Eastern schools work. He raised large sums for Oriental Christians persecuted by the Druses and carried funds to Syria himself in 1860. Rapid promotion followed: the Roman Rota in 1861, Nancy in 1863, and Algiers in March 1867. There he reversed neutrality toward Muslims, founding the White Fathers and White Sisters for orphanages, schools, hospitals, and farm settlements across the Sahara and Sudan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-edouard:
Louis Edouard Desire Pie was a French cardinal and Bishop of Poitiers, born at Pontgouin in 1815 and dead at Angouleme in 1880. Ordained in 1839, he became vicar-general of Chartres in 1844 and bishop in 1849, founding parishes, a theology faculty, and the Oblates of St. Hilary.

He is best known as an unyielding foe of modern errors and champion of church rights, scorning compromises other Catholic leaders accepted. He backed the Comte de Chambord and rebuked Napoleon III over the Papal States. At the Vatican Council he did not sign the first petition, yet became a strong defender of papal infallibility. Leo XIII made him cardinal in 1879.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mackenzie:
Mackenzie is a vicariate cut from Athabaska-Mackenzie in 1901 and entrusted to Bishop Gabriel Breynat. It is bounded west by the Rockies, south by the sixtieth parallel, east by the watershed, and open north to the pole. Over half a million square miles hold six nomad tribes, Montagnais, Slave, Flat-dog-side, Hare, Loucheux, and Eskimo, totalling 6,000 souls.

Oblates, at work since 1858, brought the Catholic faith to all but the still pagan Eskimo and some four hundred Protestants. Dog teams are the only travel, the sky the only roof, mail comes once from September to July, and provisions once a year by steamer. Living on charity, chiefly French Propagation of the Faith funds, twenty fathers and twenty-one brothers keep twelve missions, with Gray Nuns teaching orphans at Providence and Fort Resolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-madeleine-de-:
Madeleine de la Peltrie, née Chauvigny, was a French noblewoman who founded a mission, born at Caen in 1603 and dead at Quebec on 18 November 1671. Forced at seventeen to wed Charles de la Peltrie, widowed five years later, she spent ten years in piety and alms before Lejeune's Relation fired her for the Canadian mission.

Her father opposed her, so a sham courtship by de Berniere Louvigny, approved by de Condren and Vincent de Paul, left her free, and his death cancelled the union. She reached Quebec 1 August 1639 with Marie de l'Incarnation and stood sponsor at Sillery. She took first communion at Montreal's first Mass in 1642. She gave herself and her fortune wholly to the Ursuline work, never formally a novice yet living as a true religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maurice-jean-:
Maurice-Jean de Broglie, born in Paris in 1766, was the son of Field-Marshal Victor-Francois, Duc de Broglie. He studied at St-Sulpice for the priesthood. The Terror drove father and son to Berlin, where the Prussian king gave the young prince a provostship at Posen. He returned to France in 1803, and his efforts to recover family property caught Napoleon's eye. The emperor made him his almoner.

At first de Broglie hailed Napoleon as restorer of order and religion and praised him after Austerlitz. Napoleon named him Bishop of Acqui in 1805 and of Ghent in 1807. When he saw pope and clergy reduced to tools of the despot, he turned to firm opposition. By 1809 the minister of worship reported the emperor highly displeased with a bishop who would not fawn, and de Broglie died at Paris in 1821.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michiel-coxci:
Michiel Coxcie of Mechlin lived from 1499 to 1592, painting in Raphael's manner, a likeness that won him the tag of Flemish Raphael. His father taught him first, Van Orley next. He went with Van Orley to Rome in 1532, where Vasari crossed his path. There he wed Ida van Hasselt, then came home with her to Mechlin in 1539 and entered its Academy that year.

Brussels held him in 1561 before he went back to Mechlin. At seventy, in 1569, he wed Jeanne van Schelle. Ida had borne him three children: Anne, a sculptor, and William and Raphael, painters. Jeanne bore him two sons, Michiel, a painter, and Conrad. Large works for Emperor Charles V and Philip II of Spain came from his hand, and he served Philip as court painter. He drew thirty-two Cupid and Psyche scenes, later cut as prints, and ran tapestry work with Van Orley after designs by Raphael.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monastery-of-:
Corbie was a Benedictine abbey in Picardy, in the Diocese of Amiens. It was dedicated to Saints Peter and Paul and founded in 657 by Saint Bathilde, widow of Clovis II. She endowed it richly with her son Clotaire III. Its first monks came from Luxeuil under Abbot Theodefrid. Under the ninth abbot, Saint Adelhard, its school won wide fame.

Fire gutted the buildings in 1137. Commendatory abbots including Cardinal Mazarin held it from 1550. New life came in 1618 with its entry into the Congregation of Saint-Maur. Suppressed in 1790, it left its church standing with an imposing portal and towers. Its scholars included Paschasius Radbert, first to write a full treatise on the Blessed Sacrament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neal-henry-gi:
Neal Henry Gillespie was born in Washington County, Pennsylvania, on 19 January 1831, and died at Saint Mary's, Notre Dame, Indiana, on 12 November 1874. Eliza Maria Gillespie was his sister. He was among Notre Dame's earliest students, and in 1849 took its first conferred degree. On 1 September 1851 he joined the Congregation of the Holy Cross at Notre Dame as a novice.

He made his religious profession on 15 August 1853. Ordained priest at Rome on 29 June 1856, he had crossed there to complete his theology. Back in America he worked as Notre Dame's vice-president and director of studies from 1856 to 1859, then led the College of Saint Mary of the Lake in Chicago. A call took him in 1863 to the mother-house at Le Mans, France, where he stayed to 1866. Returning to Notre Dame, he took charge of the Ave Maria and kept it until his death, writing for it and for other Catholic journals too.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pearl-mary-te:
Pearl Mary Teresa Craigie, better known by the pseudonym that first won her fame, John Oliver Hobbes, was an English novelist, dramatist, and convert. She was born on 3 November 1867 and died on 13 August 1906. Eldest daughter of Boston businessman John Morgan Richards and Laura Hortense Arnold, she came of intensely Calvinist stock long settled around New York and New Jersey. Her grandfather, Reverend James Richards, was a preacher and theological writer of note.

In February 1887, before twenty, she married Reginald Walpole Craigie, an English gentleman. The union proved uncongenial, and she soon won legal separation with custody of her child. In 1892, after much private independent thought, she entered the Church. She had turned seriously to literature earlier, publishing in 1891 under her lasting pseudonym the unconventionally titled Some Emotions and a Moral. Success followed at once, with The Sinner's Comedy in 1892 and A Study in Temptations in 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-rose-u:
Pierre-Rose-Ursule-Dumoulin Borie was a French missionary bishop who was beheaded in Tongking, in what is now Vietnam, in 1838. He was born at Beynat in 1808 and trained for the foreign missions at Paris. He was ordained at Bayeux in 1830 and reached Tongking in 1832 after time at Macao.

He learned the local language fast, but a persecution edict in January 1833 forced him into hiding and hardship for most of his short mission. Captured in 1838, he learned during imprisonment that he had been named vicar apostolic of Western Tongking. He was executed with two Vietnamese priests on 24 November of that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-sebast:
Pierre-Sébastien Laurentie was a French royalist writer and campaigner for freedom of education in the nineteenth century. He was born at Houga in 1793 and came to Paris in 1817. He joined the staff of the royalist paper La Quotidienne and in 1823 became chief inspector of schools. He built a name with books on eloquence, historians, and justice.

Dismissed in 1826 after clashing with the Villèle ministry over press laws, he bought the old Benedictine college of Pontlevoy. His aim was to keep one independent school alive beside the state university monopoly. After 1830 he gave his pen wholly to three causes: free schooling, the legitimist monarchy, and the defence of religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-die:
Saint-Die is a diocese comprising the Vosges department. Suppressed in 1802 and included in Nancy, it was re-established in 1817, and in fact by a papal Bull of 1822 and a royal ordinance of 1823. The Treaty of Frankfort in 1871 cut eighteen Vosges communes to Strasburg. The diocese originated in its celebrated abbey.

St Deodatus, born toward the sixth century's close, died 679, and came from Le Nivernais or Ireland. Drawn by St Columbanus, he retired into the Vosges, stopping at Romont and Arentelle. A solitary at Wibra, persecuted by inhabitants, he went to the Vosges and founded Galilee monastery on Childeric II's lands. The town of Saint-Die now stands there. Leudin Bodo founded Bonmoutier and Etival, and Gondelbert founded Senones. These four monasteries formed a cross's extremities. Later Hidulphus erected Moyenmoutier between them at the cross's intersection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sault-sainte-:
Sault Sainte Marie, a diocese erected on 16 September 1904, covers the southern parts of Thunder Bay, Algoma, and Nipissing districts, between the height of land and Lakes Superior, Huron, and Nipissing. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with Recollect pioneers in Nipissing country.

Guillaume Poullain in 1622 and Jacques de la Foyer in 1624 spent a few months there, baptising dying children. Claude Pijart, a Jesuit, became the chief apostle of the Nipissing Algonquins and Georgian Bay peoples, labouring nine years from 1641 with Raymbault, Maynard, Gareau, Poncet, and Daran. They first preached to the Manitoulin Island tribes and as far as the Sault itself, visited by Jogues and Raymbault in 1641, where Jesuits soon planted three missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodoric-vri:
Council historian Theodoric Vrie, eyewitness to Constance, is the Augustinian chronicler described here. Brother of the Hermits of Saint Augustine and lector in sacred theology in Saxony, he modelled his history on Boethius's De consolatione philosophiae, which also supplies its original title. Narrative runs to Martin V's election and consecration on 21 November 1417.

Living still in summer 1425, he saw a general chapter at Rome authorise republication. Dialogues in prose and metre between Christ and the Church Militant present vivid facts and disorders, tracing their source and remedy. Cologne printed it in 1484 with Gerson's works, Strasburg's 1494 Gerson edition omitted it, and von der Hardt reprinted it with a short life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-ogil:
John Ogilvie was the eldest son of Walter Ogilvie of Drum near Keith in Scotland, born in 1580, who died on 10 March 1615. Brought up a Calvinist, he entered the church at Louvain through Father Cornelius a Lapide. He joined the Jesuits at seventeen, took priestly ordination in 1613, and asked to be sent on Scotland's perilous mission.

Landing in Scotland in November 1613, he reconciled many with the church in Edinburgh and Glasgow during nine months. Betrayed in Glasgow, he endured a long imprisonment in which no tortures could make him name any Catholics. Though his legs were crushed without mercy and he was kept awake nine nights by continual needle pricks, scarcely a sigh escaped him. His patience, courage, and gaiety won the admiration of his very judges, and he suffered at Glasgow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-ral:
Ralph Corbie was a Jesuit priest executed at Tyburn in September 1644. Born near Dublin in 1598 and raised from age five in northern England, he studied at St-Omer, Seville, and Valladolid. He was ordained, joined the Jesuits about 1626, and came to England about 1631 to labour at Durham.

Seized by Parliamentarians at Hamsterley in July 1644 while wearing his Mass vestments, he was carried to London and committed to Newgate with his friend John Duckett, a secular priest. At the Old Bailey both admitted their priesthood, were condemned, and were executed together on 7 September. Stonyhurst holds a relic of Corbie, and his letters survive in Foley's records of the English Jesuit province.
chesnut-diary-from-dixie:
Mary Chesnut kept her famous diary inside the Confederate elite during the Civil War. She revised it in the 1880s, and it was published in 1905 as A Diary from Dixie. Her husband was a Confederate senator and general, so she heard everything.

Chesnut records Charleston drawing rooms, Richmond gossip, and the war news reaching anxious families. She is witty about generals, sharp about slavery, and honest about dread as defeat nears. Unlike most diaries, hers reads like a novel, with scenes and dialogue rebuilt by a gifted writer. Many call it the most literary diary of the Civil War.
christmas-with-grandma-elsie:
Martha Finley published an Elsie Dinsmore holiday volume in 1888, opening in mid-November after a storm of sleet and snow. Elsie Travilla stands at her dressing-room window at Ion, delighted by trees encased in glittering ice. Her children Rosie and Walter beg for a sleighing holiday from lessons. Scripture reading together still comes first in that house.

At Woodburn, Captain Raymond and Violet weigh the same question of roads and school. The captain grants the holiday against his principles, unable to deny his family the rare treat. Family gatherings, pets lost and found, and Christmas preparations fill the middle. A lost cat and a parrot named Polly cause the evening's small alarm. Finley writes piety and affection into every parlour scene, as her series' readers expected.
contes-et-le-gendes-1re-partie:
Contes et légendes, première partie, by H. A. Guerber, is a French reader built from tales. The stories are told as simply as possible, the author explains, with endless repetition of the same words and idioms, so the pupil gains a vocabulary almost unconsciously. They are also told vividly, to arouse interest in the plot and carry the pupil to the end.

With one exception, the familiar tales are avoided, or given in unusual versions, so the sense can only be got by knowing the words. The exception comes first: The Three Bears, a common nursery story chosen on purpose. A teacher's method is outlined before the tales begin. In one, the boy Jozka, greedy and selfish, refuses the ants even a tiny piece of his mother's good cake.
dere-mable-love-letters-of-a-rookie:
Love letters from a rookie soldier fill Edward Streeter's 1918 book, written in the voice of Private Bill of the 27th, New York, Division. G. William Breck, called Bill Breck, drew the thirty-five pictures. Streeter inscribes the book to a million Private Bills who had just learnt to call a coat a blouse.

Bill writes to Mable in his own spelling, which is part of the joke. He grumbles by custom, cheers by nature, and is ever keen to be where he is not. In one letter he owns a secret: he is making a study of war, and working on a plan to end it. No one, he says, had gone into how to quit it. The book was a home-front hit of the war year.
dick-and-brownie:
A child's escape from a caravan fills Mabel Quiller-Couch's tale of Dick and Brownie. Twelve chapters carry the story from the escape to happy hours. A summer sun blazes on a white road and moorland as it opens, and the only shade is a small coppice.

In that shade sleep four live things: a man, a woman, a horse, and a dog, the dirtiest group for miles. Huldah, the child, flees them with the dog. Miss Rose, met on the road, takes her part, and buys her a cloak in a shop scene of wonder. Tracked down, rescued, and given a new home fill the later chapters. The tale is a warm, simple story of a bad home left and a good one found.
doe-osti-2574490-combining-genome-wide-a:
A final scientific report led by Gail Taylor of UC Davis, with Jin-Gui Chen and Wellington Muchero of Oak Ridge as co-investigators, hunts the genes behind drought tolerance in poplar trees. Poplar is a leading bioenergy crop, and water limits where it can grow. The team combined a huge field trial with genome-wide association mapping and expression mapping to find the networks involved.

The trial planted 1,382 Populus trichocarpa genotypes on a 6.1 hectare site at Davis, split between drought and full irrigation blocks. Association studies in two poplar species were compared, and RNA sequencing under both treatments located expression-controlling variants. Up to fifty hub variants were checked in protoplast assays, and gene editing protocols for poplar were established. Most objectives closed fully complete. The cross-species comparison and final candidate gene validation remain active, the report notes.
doe-osti-2588213-rationally-designed-lit:
Henry Costantino of Group14 Technologies led this project report on next generation lithium-ion battery anodes. The funding ran from October 2020 through December 2024 and totaled about 4.78 million dollars, with the Department of Energy covering about 3.76 million. Partners included Cabot Corporation, Silatronix, Arkema, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, and Farasis Energy. The aim stated in the title is blunt: batteries good enough to displace internal combustion engines.

The centerpiece is Group14's silicon-carbon composite anode material. In earlier work it gave 35 percent higher energy density when blended at 12 percent with graphite, over 1,000 cycles of stability, and a projected cell cost under 125 dollars per kilowatt-hour. This project pushed toward anodes with at least 30 percent silicon-carbon composite. Each partner tuned a matching piece: Cabot the carbon additives, Arkema the binders, Silatronix the electrolyte co-solvents, and PNNL the test support.
doe-osti-3002218-automated-segmentation-:
Bryan Conry, Grant W. Helmreich, and Tyler J. Gerczak teach software to read fuel micrographs in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4100, dated September 2025. The fuel is TRISO, a coated particle fuel for high-temperature gas reactors. Its silicon carbide layer holds back fission products, and the layer's grain structure affects how well it works. Twin boundaries, mirror-image seams inside grains, skew the usual grain measurements.

The team trained a deep neural network to find twin boundaries in electron microscope images. Removing the twins lets quality metrics be recomputed, including for older data sets. Tests used both simulated images and real backscattered electron images of the carbide layer. Threshold settings near 0.4 to 0.45 shaped the final twin maps. The tool aims at faster, more uniform quality checks for fuel production.
doe-osti-3003141-continuous-baseline-mic:
M. Wang, K. Johnson, A. Zhou, S. E. Giangrande, and M. Jensen, all at Brookhaven, document a long-running data product in ARM report DOE/SC-ARM-TR-095, dated November 2025. The product is MICROBASE, a continuous retrieval of cloud microphysical properties: droplet sizes, water contents, and related quantities, computed from radar and radiometer observations. Cloud modelers use it as a steady baseline record.

The report describes the retrieval method and its uncertainty treatment, including a perturbation method for quantifying errors in cloud property retrievals. It sits in the ARM value-added product line, where raw instrument streams become analysis-ready data. Wang and Zhou are credited as developers, Giangrande as translator, Johnson and Jensen as science sponsors. Updated documentation matters because the product's record stretches across many ARM sites and years of data.
doe-osti-3004457-measurements-and-analys:
Lynn M. Russell of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography reports for DOE project DE-SC0022958, which supported the Eastern Pacific Cloud Aerosol Precipitation Experiment. EPCAPE studied marine stratocumulus clouds off La Jolla, California. The site sits about a day downwind of the Los Angeles and Long Beach port pollution sources. That placement gives a wide range of particle levels under persistent cloud decks, a natural laboratory for aerosol-cloud science.

The project provided measurements and analyses behind the campaign's science: cloud extent, radiative properties, precipitation, and how manmade particles alter them. Seasonal cycles in cloud and aerosol properties were a focus. Data products include curated campaign data sets with public identifiers, and trajectory data sets that augment the ARM facility's records. Cloud modelers use such paired records to test how pollution shifts cloud brightness.
doe-osti-3012841-restoring-homes-after-w:
Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report by Wanyu R. Chan, Ada Lee, and Hugo Destaillats, dated January 2026, gathers what professional cleaners know about restoring homes after wildfires. The study, funded through an interagency agreement with the Environmental Protection Agency, rests on interviews with remediation practitioners. It asks what cleanup steps they take, what drives their choices, and where their knowledge runs out.

Health concerns and odor removal emerged as the main motivations for remediation work. Practitioners agreed that thorough physical cleaning is the most important first step, and that smoke-soaked insulation often has to come out. The interviews also compare odor treatments such as ozone and hydroxyl generators, where firms disagreed about safety and effectiveness. The findings map the guidance and research that homeowners still lack.
doe-osti-3021514-roadmap-to-advance-heli:
Roadmap report NLR/TP-5700-97216, by Steve Schell, Guangdong Zhu, and co-authors from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, Sandia, and Australian universities, updates the Heliostat Consortium's plan for cheaper solar-thermal technology. Heliostats are fields of sun-tracking mirrors that concentrate light onto a receiver for power generation or industrial heat. The consortium's 2022 roadmap named the gaps; this 2026 report measures progress and resets priorities for high-temperature systems.

Six topic areas structure the work: techno-economic analysis, metrology and standards, components and controls, advanced manufacturing, resources and training, and field deployment, with wind load and soiling as special subtopics. Progress since 2022 includes better optical measurement, new standards work, and training programs. One detailed thread pursues composite mirror facets: a 1-millimeter mirror raises reflectivity from about 93 to 96 percent, but needs a sandwich backing to stay durable.
doe-osti-3021606-enabling-high-gradient-:
Illinois Institute of Technology final report for DOE grant DE-SC0022057, led by Eric Wisniewski and submitted March 4, 2026, reports the first high-power, short-pulse tests of Dielectric Disk Accelerators. These electron accelerating structures replace some metal with dielectric disks, gaining efficiency and letting fields build up faster. Faster buildup means shorter radio-frequency pulses, and shorter pulses reduce electrical breakdown, the usual ceiling on accelerating gradient.

Two traveling-wave structures, single-cell and multicell, ran at 11.7 gigahertz at the Argonne Wakefield Accelerator, powered by 9-nanosecond pulses from a wakefield source. The multicell structure reached 222 megawatts of peak power and a gradient near 80 megavolts per meter with no breakdown. A standing-wave version tested at KEK in Japan took over 20 megawatts before a ceramic disk was damaged. The report judges the short-pulse traveling-wave design ready for further development.
doe-osti-3029947-retention-of-ldr-inorga:
David Blumenkranz and Rod Skeen of Hanford Tank Waste Operations and Closure sum up lab work in report RPP-RPT-66455, published in April 2026. Hanford tank waste will be locked into a cement-like solid for offsite disposal. Federal land disposal rules cover 13 inorganic species in that waste, and each shipment would normally need sampling after treatment to prove it passes leach tests. The team seeks a rule variance that drops that slow step.

Their path uses retention factors: the share of each species the solid keeps. Data across formulas gave one lower-bound factor per species at 95 percent confidence. Four species, silver, arsenic, barium, and selenium, often fell below 95 percent retention. Only cadmium, chromium, mercury, and lead are forecast to need any retention credit at all.
doe-osti-3030036-opportunities-to-expand:
Noah Sandoval, Sletsy Dlamini, and Allison Moe of the National Laboratory of the Rockies look at workforce training in report NLR/TP-5500-94704, dated April 2026. More than 2.3 million United States workers do jobs that cut building energy use, per the latest federal energy and employment count. They span design, construction, and system upkeep. The report asks how community colleges can grow their share of training for that workforce.

Reading and case studies surfaced five main hurdles. First, job data often miss these roles, since many hide inside broader trade labels, so colleges struggle to prove employer demand to their own leaders. Other hurdles cover funding, staffing, and keeping programs current. For each hurdle the authors offer workable fixes drawn from schools already running such programs.
doe-osti-3377982-building-a-high-through:
Building a High-Throughput MiniFuel PIE Pipeline for HFIR-Based Advanced Fuel Evaluation, Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2026/4475 from July 2026, sets up a faster way to examine small test fuels after irradiation. Eleven authors are printed, led by A. G. Le Coq, D. Adorno Lopes, and S. E. Trewhitt. The work carries milestone number M3FT-26OR020201042 and sits in the Advanced Fuels Campaign.

MiniFuel tests use small fuel specimens irradiated in the High Flux Isotope Reactor, HFIR, so many candidate fuels can be screened at once. PIE, post-irradiation examination, is the bottleneck afterward: each specimen must be measured and characterized. The report describes building that examination into a pipeline with enough throughput to keep pace with the reactor's output, so advanced fuel evaluation is not limited by the lab bench.
doe-osti-3484700-evidence-and-judgment-a:
Argonne book-length report ANL-26/23, by Benjamin Blakely, weighs how AI should be used in mission work, without hype or dismissal. The title frames the stance: evidence and judgment. A long acronym list opens the volume, from AI benchmarks to computing terms.

One key split separates grounding from mere lack of false claims. A claim can be true in general yet fail grounding if it fights the user's source set. Retrieval systems that cite set sources are the standard fix named. Agencies get a careful frame for when AI answers deserve trust.
doe-osti-3520353-status-of-astm-d8289-op:
Oak Ridge letter report ORNL/LTR-2026/4732, by Lianshan Lin and Nidia C. Gallego and dated August 2026, updates optimization studies for ASTM standard D8289. The standard covers tensile testing of graphite with small disc samples. Graphite grades vary widely, so test details matter.

Charts compare splitting tensile strength against uniaxial tensile strength across grades. Full-field strain maps show how disc surfaces deform during loading. Fine-grained graphite such as Mersen 2114 strains differently from coarse grades. Pictures of strain fields expose those gaps clearly. Standards writers can tune the test so results compare fairly across graphite types.
doe-osti-3912523-nsls-ii-radioactive-sam:
Brookhaven technical note NSLSII-ESH-TN-453, dated August 28, 2026, tests Monte Carlo radiation fields for radioactive samples at a light source. Seven authors are printed, led by Ricardo dos Santos Augusto. Demand for radioactive sample experiments at the National Synchrotron Light Source II has grown fast. Each sample must be characterized so protection staff can plan safe handling and measurement. Dose estimates today come from analytic formulas based on activity alone.

For hotter samples, those estimates may not support the shielding plans now needed. The team ran FLUKA calculations for samples bare and shielded, mapping the fields staff would face. Simulated values were set against the protection office's own estimates. One finding is stark: inside the hutch, contact dose rates for the strongest class would be unacceptable without added shielding. The aim throughout is doses as low as reasonably achievable.
elizabethan-demonology-an-essay-in-illus:
Thomas Alfred Spalding, a barrister and officer of the New Shakspere Society, explains what Elizabethans believed about devils in an essay printed at London in 1880 and dedicated to Robert Browning. The book grew from two papers read to the society in 1877 and 1878, on the witches in Macbeth and the demonology of Shakspere. Quotations from Charles Lamb and Carlyle front the argument.

Spalding holds that we cannot read the elder writers without their ideas. He traces the powers granted to devils, the kinds of spirits, and the signs of witchcraft in the age's own books. One passage lists how the deadly sins were pictured: envy by disdainful looks, wrath by furious gestures, gluttony by vomiting, and sloth by snorting as if asleep. The essay serves Shakespeare readers who meet devils on every third page and want the creed behind them.
evangeline-a-tale-of-acadie:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's Evangeline, A Tale of Acadie opens in the forest primeval, among murmuring pines and hemlocks standing like Druids of eld. Below them once stood Grand-Pre, the Acadian village the British destroyed in 1755. Evangeline Bellefontaine and Gabriel Lajeunesse are betrothed on the very eve of the expulsion.

The poem follows Evangeline's lifelong search down the Mississippi and across America, through churchyards and towns, always just missing Gabriel, until she finds him dying in a Philadelphia almshouse. Longfellow wrote in hexameters learned from Homer and Goethe. Published in 1847, the poem made the Acadian tragedy famous worldwide and fixed Longfellow as America's household poet for a century.
eyes-of-youth-a-book-of-verse-by-padraic:
Various poets fill Eyes of Youth, a book of verse by young writers of its day. Padraic Colum and Shane Leslie head the named list of contributors. Viola Meynell, Ruth Lindsay, and Francis Meynell also appear. Gilbert K. Chesterton wrote the foreword. Four early poems by Francis Thompson appear in book form for the first time here.

The contents open with Thompson's Threatened Tears and Arab Love Song. Buona Notte and The Passion of Mary complete his group. Colum offers An Idyll, Christ the Comrade, and two Arab Songs. Leslie's pieces include A Dead Friend and Fleet Street Nightmare. A line from The Merry Wives of Windsor gives the book its title. The anthology catches a literary generation in its youth.
field-and-hedgerow-being-the-last-essays:
Richard Jefferies's Field and Hedgerow gathers his last essays, collected by his widow after his death. The essays first appeared in the Fortnightly Review, the Manchester Guardian, the Pall Mall Gazette, the Standard, Longman's Magazine and other periodicals of the day.

Contents include Hours of Spring, The July Grass, Winds of Heaven, Swallow-Time, Walks in the Wheat-Fields, Field Words and Ways, Cottage Ideas, and Summer in Somerset. Jefferies writes of Sussex, deer-parks, old villages and birds' nests with the close observation that made him famous. Readers who love English nature writing will find Field and Hedgerow a fitting, autumnal close to his work.
forty-one-years-in-india-from-subaltern-:
Roberts recounts a career that ran the whole ladder of British India, from subaltern to commander-in-chief. The two volumes sold through edition after edition in the first weeks of 1897. His service covered mutiny, frontier campaigns, and the high command of an army.

One set piece describes a cyclone striking Calcutta. His transports on the river came through with only two damaged, but the native bazaar lay levelled under feet of water. Great trees were torn up by the roots and houses split clean down the middle. Frederick Sleigh Roberts, later Earl Roberts, published the memoir in January 1897.
georgie:
Jacob Abbott wrote Georgie for the Rollo Story Books, published in 1857 for young children. Georgie lives in a pleasant house under a hill, near the stone bridge over the brook, in Rollo's neighborhood. A large apple tree by the house bears sweet golden pippins. Short chapters carry titles such as Georgie's Money, Two Good Friends, and A Lecture on Playthings.

Each small tale turns on a child's daily act: spending a coin, sharing a toy, or driving a toy cart. Abbott slips a short tale of Shallow, Selfish, and Wise into the fun. The lessons are plain but kindly told, in the manner of his Rollo books. Parents of the time read these aloud to teach care and good temper by story rather than scolding.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrackenEddie_Br: nsia-BrackenEddie Bracken Eddie: the made public government document on Eddie Bracken, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, of the files. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EbanErnie_Eban_: A letter written in December 1976 to a man named Ernie opens with an apology for a delayed reply. The writer then turns to business: efforts to persuade David Belin to support a new investigation. Belin had served on the Warren Commission staff. The author's name cannot be recovered, so the letter survives as an unsigned snapshot of researchers lobbying for a reopened inquiry in 1976.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-EdmundsonDennie: nsia-EdmundsonDennie Edmundson Dennie: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RachleyVirgie_R: nsia-RachleyVirgie Rachley Virgie: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-YatesDixie_Yate: An FBI memo from 1975 records information Dixie Yates gave the Dallas office by telephone about the JFK assassination. Twelve years after the shooting, citizens still called in tips and memories. The bureau still wrote them down. The Yates memo is a late entry in a file that never fully closed, showing how long the assassination kept generating new paper.
grandmother-elsie:
Martha Finley's Elsie books were among the most loved girls' stories of the 1800s, and Grandmother Elsie, a sequel to Elsie's Widowhood, carries the tale into a third generation. This authorized edition follows the copy of 1882. The Ion family are home again after a summer on the New Jersey coast, as the first chapter opens on a bright October morning at their lawn and lakelet.

Elsie, now a grandmother, guides children and grandchildren with her firm, gentle faith. Family trials, travel, and daily worship fill the book, in Finley's earnest manner. Her readers wept and prayed with Elsie for decades. Modern readers may find the piety strong, yet the books shaped the ideals of countless girls. This volume shows the matriarch at the center of a wide, loving clan.
heralds-of-empire-being-the-story-of-one:
Agnes C Laut published this historical novel at Toronto in 1902. Ramsay Stanhope tells the tale in his own voice. He serves Pierre Radisson in the northern fur trade. Their world is Hudson Bay, rival traders, and hard winter travel.

Stanhope looks back on plots, rescues, and fights for furs and forts. French, English, and native peoples meet as allies and foes. Laut frames the trade as the seed of a new world order in Canada. Readers get a bold, old-style adventure built on the real push for the bay.
indiscretions-of-archie:
P. G. Wodehouse set his farce Indiscretions of Archie in a grand New York hotel, where a penniless Englishman has married the owner's daughter. Archie Moffam wed Lucille Brewster for love, with neither money nor a job to offer. Daniel Brewster, the hotel proprietor and father-in-law, has never forgiven Archie for once criticizing his hotel. George H. Doran published the book in 1921.

Chapters chain Archie's blundering good deeds into fresh disasters for the Brewster household. He hunts for work, poses as an artist's model, and tangles with a bomb plot scare. Brother Bill's romance, a sausage seller, and young Washy finding fame fill the middle episodes. Reggie, Looney Biddle, and Mr. Connolly each get a turn in the machinery. The Wigmore Venus, a statue with a past, drives the closing mix-ups. Wodehouse keeps every scrape light, fast, and forgiven by the final page, in his early manner.
keeping-up-with-lizzie:
Keeping Up with Lizzie is Irving Bacheller's novel of a small town turned upside down, published by Harper in March 1911. W. L. Jacobs illustrated it, and Bacheller dedicates it to Mr. Onedear. In Pointview, the tradesmen form a sort of board of assessors. Lizzie, newly back from travel abroad, has met a queen and gained an accent and a fiancé.

Her return sets off a race of spending and showing off among her old neighbors. The ham war and flying visits fill the middle chapters. The Honorable Socrates Potter, the town's shrewd lawyer, finally catches up with Lizzie in the last. Bacheller satirizes small-town pride through one girl's rise and everyone's scramble to match it.
lady-connie:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published her novel Lady Connie in 1916. Albert Sterner drew its pictures. The book runs in three parts and nineteen chapters.

Constance, called Connie, stands at the center of the story. A picture caption shows her entranced by music at a tea party. Another shows her with Falloden at her feet under a plane tree. Ward mixes romance with serious talk about duty and character. Readers who like her thoughtful social novels will find that blend here. Ward's heroines often face a test of conscience. Connie's story follows that pattern within Oxford and country house settings.
literary-hearthstones-of-dixie:
La Salle Corbell Pickett published this tour of Southern literary homes in 1912. J. B. Lippincott issued it with portraits and illustrations. Pickett also wrote Pickett and His Men and Jinny. Her foreword finds fires still glowing on old hearthstones.

Southern writers once welcomed friends at those firesides, she writes. Gifted pens there gave voice to readers' own unspoken thoughts. The builders of those shrines have passed from the world. Pickett tends their memory for a later generation of readers. Four feet on the fender recalled talks with gifted friends. Heart's-blood pens, Pickett writes, voiced readers' own flaming thoughts.
love-letters-of-a-rookie-to-julie:
Love Letters of a Rookie to Julie is a comic war book by Barney Stone. Stone served with Headquarters Company, 119th Field Artillery, in France. The book, copyrighted in 1919, prints his letters home to Julie. Gordon Ross drew the funny pictures that go with them.

The rookie writes in cheerful, mangled spelling from camp and trench. He tells of the train ride, the farewell at Julie's flat, and army food. His slang and mix-ups carry the humor of a green soldier. Real affection for Julie runs under all the jokes. The letters give a light, human view of the American doughboy.
marie:
Marie is a story by Laura E. Richards, published in 1894. Richards also wrote Captain January and Queen Hildegarde. Her Marie has walked nearly the whole day as the sun sinks. Long rays rest on farmhouse windows and tree-tops like fiddle-bows.

Marie thinks in music, and hugs her treasure close as a baby. She has run away from the troupe she traveled with. The face of 'Le Boss' still makes her shiver in memory. Ahead lies a New England village, a kind family, and a new life. Chapters promise courtship, wedlock, and a vita nuova — a new life. Richards tells it with her usual warmth and grace.
mary-marie:
Eleanor H. Porter published Mary Marie in 1920. Helen Mason Grose drew the pictures for the book. A short preface says it will explain things at the start.

The heroine tells her own tale, from the words I Am Born. Nurse Sarah's story comes next, then the break in the home. Some chapters call her Mary, some Marie, and some both at once. That split name frames her search for which self is the real one. A test and a true love story wait near the end. Porter lets the girl's own voice carry both grief and hope.
mince-pie:
Christopher Morley collected these humorous sketches from the newspapers where they first appeared. Most ran in the Philadelphia Evening Public Ledger. Others came from The Bookman, the Boston Evening Transcript, Life, and The Smart Set. His instructions order the book to be read in bed, and never from a borrowed copy.

Morley calls the pieces trifles and offers no excuse for prolonging their existence. He hopes a copy on the bedside shelf may pave the way to easy slumber. The sketches include a mock account of a president traveling abroad. Morley's light essays show the daily newspaper humor column at its most genial.
mischievous-maid-faynie:
Laura Jean Libbey published this dime-novel romance in an author's special edition in 1899. The story opens during a terrible New York blizzard. Snow buries Broadway, cable cars stall, and two handsome young men breast the storm together. Strangers take them for twin brothers, but they are only cousins.

One cousin is Clinton Kendale, the actor everyone calls the rage of New York. The other is Lester Armstrong, an assistant cashier with no great hopes. Libbey wrote popular romances like Ione and Parted by Fate for working readers. Snow, stage fame, and a mischievous maid drive this tale of love and mistaken standing.
miss-dexie:
Stanford Eveleth published this Canadian novel at Toronto in 1895. He subtitles it A Romance of the Provinces. The introduction is dated 1864, in wartime. News of the American Civil War fills a New England town with grief and argument, as casualty lists grow daily.

Wives' and mothers' faces whiten as men hurry to telegraph offices for news. Eveleth, published by William Briggs with agents in Montreal and Halifax, wrote for readers across the young Dominion. His romance crosses the border in feeling: Canadians watching a neighboring republic tear itself apart. The provinces' own loyalties and families carry the story forward.
mother-s-remedies-over-one-thousand-trie:
Dr. Thomas Jefferson Ritter compiled this vast book of home cures from mothers across the United States and Canada. Its title promises over one thousand tried and tested remedies. The transcriber's notes warn modern readers first. Recipes call for kerosene, turpentine, lead, lye, strychnine, arsenic, mercury, opium, and cocaine.

Poultices appear in hundreds of recipes, and keeping the bowels open in nearly fifteen hundred. The transcriber calls the book a window into mothers' terror when a child fell ill. Doctors of the era could often offer little more. As social history, the volume is unmatched; as medicine, it belongs firmly to its time.
nasa-tm-19680020515-high-temperature-cre:
Robert J. Buzzard of Lewis Research Center measured creep-rupture strength in a tungsten and uranium dioxide cermet for this 1968 report. The material mixes equal volumes of tungsten and uranium dioxide. It was made by roll compaction of tungsten-coated uranium dioxide particles, then clad with tungsten.

Tests ran at very high temperatures under steady stress until samples broke. Rupture lives ranged from about one hour to hundreds of hours, depending on heat and load. Buzzard used the Manson-Haferd parameter to predict longer-term behavior and creep stages. He also examined what role the uranium dioxide plays in the failure process. The tungsten phase seemed to control strength and ductility.
podcast-tuckercarlson-r_Vt_Lo5SiE:
Independent researcher Ian Carroll joins Tucker Carlson to revisit America's deadliest mass shooting, the 2017 Las Vegas attack. Carroll built a following by questioning official stories in viral videos. Here he airs the unanswered questions he says authorities do not want asked.

Carroll walks through the timeline gaps, witness accounts, and evidence disputes in the case. He asks why the motive was never settled in public. Carlson, who has covered the story's odd turns before, presses for what a real inquiry would need. Questioning viewers get a citizen's probe into a case that still unsettles the country.
poems-c-1790-wherein-it-is-attempted-to-:
London readers in 1790 could buy an anonymous volume whose title page promises poems attempting to describe certain views of nature and of rustic manners. To show how the same circumstances affect different characters differently. Printed for J. Johnson in St. Paul's Churchyard, the book carries no author's name, only its program: close observation of country life, rendered in verse, with an eye on human variety.

The opening poem, A Winter Day, begins before dawn with the cock crowing among his hens. Then follows the laboring hind who dreams of gold from next year's crop and wakes to find himself the same poor man. Detail piles up lovingly: straw beds, home-spun coverings, the smothered fire blown back to life. The volume belongs to the late-century turn toward realistic rural poetry that prepared the way for Wordsworth and Clare.
sir-gibbie:
George MacDonald wrote this Scots novel around a small, saintly boy called Gibbie. Contents run through thirty-one chapters, from The Earring and Sir George to Mistress Croale and The Parlour. A glossary of broad Scots, added by the electronic text's maker, stands at the end to help with the dialogue.

Later heads promise Gibbie adrift, a barn refuge, Donal Grant, apprenticeship, and secret service. MacDonald sets a child of pure heart among drunks, lairds, and gamekeepers in the Scottish hills. Love and quiet goodness, not force, carry Gibbie through a hard world that keeps misreading him.
sister-carrie:
Theodore Dreiser published this novel with Doubleday, Page in New York in 1900 and dedicated it to his friend Arthur Henry. A copied hand-written note at the front thanks a Mr. Norris for early, full approval of the story in draft. Dreiser credits that backing for the book reaching print so soon.

Carrie, a young woman from the country, rides toward Chicago's lights in the tale that follows. Work, hunger, the stage, and kept luxury test her in turn. Dreiser's first novel shocked its age with a heroine who rises by paths that polite fiction condemned, and it still anchors talk on American realism.
t-mann-buddenbrooks-verfall-einer-famili:
Four generations of Luebeck merchants rise and fall in Buddenbrooks, given here in Mann's original German as Buddenbrooks: Verfall einer Familie. Published in 1901, the novel made its twenty-six-year-old author world-famous. Its subtitle announces the theme: the decline of a family, tracked across a century of trade.

In Mann's own language, the prose shows the irony and music that translation can only suggest. Business ledgers and family Bibles record christenings, marriages, failures, and deaths in equal detail. Vitality ebbs from commerce into art as the generations pass. The book eventually carried its author to the Nobel Prize. German readers still meet it young and return to it for life.
the-arte-of-english-poesie:
Printed at London by Richard Field in the Blackfriars in 1589, The Arte of English Poesie divides its craft into three books: of poets and poetry, of proportion, and of ornament. No author's name stands on the title page. A shield shows a hand coming out of a cloud and gripping an anchor twined with vine.

Field the printer addresses the book to Sir William Cecil, Lord Burghley, high treasurer of England. He admits the book came to his hands with its bare title only, no author and no address. Many passages showed it was meant for the Queen's own pastime and service, he says, which made him doubt whether he should present it to any other person at all.
the-awakening-of-helena-richie:
Margaret Deland dated her novel May 12, 1906, and linked it to her earlier Dr Lavendar's People. Dr Lavendar drives his horse Goliath up a muddy hill in Old Chester to call on old Benjamin Wright. He dislikes the duty but tells his small dog Daniel that pastoral calls are not about liking.

On the way home he passes the Stuffed Animal House, once owned by a taxidermist, where Mrs Frederick Richie watches his buggy go by. Wright, lonely and sharp-tongued, has not spoken to his only son Samuel for more than thirty years. Small-town duty, old quarrels, and a widow's watchful life set the scene.
the-german-classics-of-the-nineteenth-an: Kuno Francke edited The German Classics, a twenty-volume set of German masterworks in English dress, and this first volume was printed at Albany in 1913. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. The volume opens with a life of Goethe, then his poems in versions by Charles Wharton Stork and E. A. Bowring, among them Prometheus and The Heathrose. No full work is included in this portion, so the texts cannot be told from these opening pages alone.
the-lesser-bourgeoisie:
Honore de Balzac dedicated his novel of the Paris middle classes to Constance-Victoire in a playful letter. He says Moliere left a few scraps of clay unused when he built Tartuffe, and Balzac kneaded those scraps into a modern hypocrite. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the book into English, as its title page states.

Part one follows the lesser bourgeois of Paris, opening at the tourniquet Saint-Jean, a narrow passage into the city. Balzac studies clerks, widows, and place seekers who scheme for small gains and thin respect. His comedy stays sharp about money, rank, and self deception in a crowded capital.
the-marquis-of-lossie: George MacDonald wrote The Marquis of Lossie. Only the title page and contents are present, so the novel does not appear. The forty-four chapter titles begin in a stable-yard and a library, introduce Miss Horn, a horse named Kelpie, Lizzy Findlay, and Mr. Crathie, then travel: Voyage to London, London Streets, The Tempest, and Kelpie in London. Later titles include The Schoolmaster, The Preacher, The Portrait, An Evil Omen, A Quarrel, The Two Daimons, Lies, An Old Enemy, and a final chapter, The Mind of the Author.
the-pigeon-pie: Charlotte M. Yonge's The Pigeon Pie is shown here in the new edition published by A. R. Mowbray and Co. in 1905. The firm had offices in Oxford and London. Here only the title page and the start of the contents appear, so the story itself is absent. The contents list chapters by number and page only, Chapter I at page 1 and Chapter V at page 62. A sibling record of the same 1905 edition carries the same front matter and then goes on into the first chapter.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol:
Earlier Poems, 1830 to 1836, form the opening section of The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes in the 1893 three-volume set. A contents list names Old Ironsides, The Last Leaf, and The Cambridge Churchyard. It also names To an Insect, The Dilemma, My Aunt, The Dorchester Giant, and The Comet. The Music-Grinders, The September Gale, and The Last Reader follow, closing with Poetry: A Metrical Essay.

Before them stands a short verse address to his readers. Holmes asks not to be blamed for sparing their patience many a trivial verse. The earlier poems once shared a welcome, and the better may shield the worse. Some readers, he admits, may find a freshness in the ruder songs that newer work has lost. The lines turn on his own ageing. When those poems were written his locks were brown; the ones he writes now belong to autumn.
the-prairie:
James Fenimore Cooper's The Prairie is framed by a contents list of thirty-four chapters and two introductions. An opening note states that the novel was the third in order of Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales. It first appeared in 1827. The note begins a short account of the book's place in the series before the tale itself starts.

Readers who know the series will place the story from that note alone. The prairie setting carries the Leatherstocking figure west, far from the forests of the earlier tales. The bare chapter numbers in the contents give no hint of scenes or persons. All the weight of the opening falls on the introductions, which set out the book's standing in Cooper's long frontier sequence.
the-princess-and-curdie: George MacDonald's The Princess and Curdie is shown through its contents and the bare heading of Chapter 1. The chapters themselves are not on view. Thirty-five chapters are listed, opening with The Mountain, The White Pigeon, and The Mistress of the Silver Moon. Curdie's father and mother, the miners, and the emerald follow. Middle titles include Curdie's Mission, Lina, The Dogs of Gwyntystorm, and The King's Kitchen. The Lord Chamberlain, Dr. Kelman, and The Prophecy lead toward The Avengers, The Sacrifice, The Battle, and Judgement.
the-spanish-tragedie: Thomas Kyd's revenge tragedy, dated 1587, appears in a text based on the earliest extant edition. John Matthews Manly edited it in 1897. A transcriber's note explains choices among editions and the exclusion of passages once supposed to be by Ben Jonson. The pages present here carry that note and the old title. The title promises the lamentable end of Don Horatio and Bel-imperia. A cast list begins with the ghost of Andrea, so the play itself does not appear.
the-story-of-jessie:
Mabel Quiller-Couch wrote this children's story in twelve chapters. The chapters begin with a letter for Sunnyside Cottage. Jessie's arrival and happy days follow. A journey and a new home come next. A final return to Springbrook closes the book. Chapter one opens in the Dawsons' kitchen. Thomas Dawson is busy there. He tries to make the kettle boil. He clears the fire so he can make a piece of toast.

Thomas has already tidied the grate. He has swept the floor too. He stands with the loaf in one hand. He is about to cut a slice. His eye wanders down the dewy, sunny garden. Every tree and bush shows the first green film on its brown branches. The spring morning prepares the cottage. The letter and the child of the title are on their way.
valerie:
Captain Frederick Marryat's novel Valerie, dated 1848, carries a preface that tells how the book was made. On August 10, 1845, Marryat wrote to a lady friend urging her to write her confessions, which he offered to publish. He had notes on the early life of a Frenchwoman, cast adrift at seventeen, and wanted to work her story together with the lady's own. Washington Irving, the preface says, had once wished to join in the same plan.

The lady declined, and the tale went ahead without her. It ran in the New Monthly in 1846 and 1847 under Marryat's hand for its first eleven chapters, as Mademoiselle Virginie. When it became a book called Valerie, another hand added the closing pages after his death. Readers get a French heroine's life story with an unusual birth: part magazine serial, part posthumous finish, explained frankly at the front.
winston-of-the-prairie: The front pages here give the title page and a partial contents list for Harold Bindloss's Winston of the Prairie, printed in 1907, with no story text present. W. Herbert Dunton drew the pictures. The frontispiece shows a man on foot urging a team through powdery snow drifts. The contents open with Rancher Winston and Lance Courthorne. A trooper's quarrel and Miss Barrington's homecoming follow. Winston comes to Silverdale, and Courthorne disappears, in the list. A promise by Maud Barrington and plowing fill later titles.
